Mr. Speaker, I rise today to commend the farmers from Ontario and Quebec who were here on Parliament Hill yesterday to try to make this government understand that its policy direction is unacceptable for Canadian agriculture and will end in the destruction of this once vibrant industry.
Those thousands of fanners who conducted this demonstration with purpose and dignity and their forceful presentation should make this government realize that the free trade agreement has already proven to be a disaster to Canadian farmers and Canadian food processors.
We have had a countervail placed against our pork entering the United States from Canada. We have a threat of countervail against our Durum wheat entering the United States. We have a GATT decision against our dairy farmers allowing ice cream and yoghurt into Canada, while the United States restricts imports of our ice cream into their country. Just last week the St. Lawrence Starch Company announced that it was closing its plant in Ontario and moving to Buffalo, New York.
This government has been systematically dismantling the most sophisticated marketing system of any country in the world and Canadian farmers are being thrown to the vultures of the market-place.
I call on this government today to stop this madness, to restore agriculture to the position that it deserves in society, to restore the Advance Payments for Crops programs, to provide its share of crop insurance premiums to make it truly tripartite, to restore At and East transportation policy, and to restore the Farm Credit
Corporation as a credible lending agency rather than a collection agency.
I call on this government to make agriculture a national security issue and give the Canadian farmers who demonstrated here yesterday a secure living that is commensurate with that of the rest of society.

Mr. Speaker, in my riding office, I regularly receive people in search of employment, as do my colleagues in this House I suppose.
In recent years, I have noticed a lack of coordination between employers and potential employees.
Mr. Speaker, more and more employers lack skilled workers and must make do with fewer employees than they need. At the same time, prospective employees only have such general training with no specific skills that they conclude few jobs are available.
Some say that there are no jobs, but I wonder! Take a look in the Canada Employment Centres where jobs are posted. There are jobs, and I am convinced that a very small effort in terms of training would create openings for them that they do not even suspect exist.
Once job seekers understand that employers' needs go beyond the status quo, we will train a society that can meet our expectations.

Mr. Speaker, we hear today that the armed conflict between the military in El Salvador and the opposition forces continues to escalate. The Liberal party believes that Canada can no longer take a passive stand in light of these dramatic developments. We would like to ensure that the Canadian government immediately addresses the following recommendations.
First, that the Canadian government through its new role in the OAS urge the United States to reconsider its policy on El Salvador and in that context suspend its aid to the Salvadoran military and condition its economic aid to political negotiations, human rights and compliance with the Esquipulas II peace accord.
Second, encourage the OAS, specifically its human rights arm, to investigate the human rights abuses in El Salvador and report as soon as possible, as well as call on El Salvador's government to cease and desist immediately from human rights violations.
Third, that Canada adopt an open-door policy for refugees escaping the conflict in El Salvador during this time of crisis and hardship and put a moratorium on the deportation of any El Salvadoran refugees now living in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, an unacceptable case of toxic contamination exists in the community of Rankin Inlet in my constituency in the Northwest Territories. The contamination has been found in the tailings pond of an abandoned nickel mine. The results of a consultant's report show that the level of contamination for arsenic, copper, nickel and sulphur exceeds the severe contamination level.
The report suggests that for the past 20 to 30 years the tailings area has probably been generating an acidified leachate which has drained into the marine waters of Rankin Inlet. It points to possible problems arising from heavy metal accumulation in sediments and the food chain.
The consultants say that more detailed investigations to assess the nature and extent of the contamination and the associated health risks to the community are needed as soon as possible.
I call upon the Government of Canada to exercise its environmental responsibilities and act upon its expressed concern for the Canadian Arctic environment. Get involved, clean up the contamination now.

Mr. Speaker, on November 13, this year, Canadians heard the sad news of the tragic death of one of our most famous athletes.
A gold and silver medal winner at the 1984 Olympic Games and three times winner of the world record for the 200 metre breast stroke, Victor Davis was throughout his career and his all too short life a shining example of courage and determination and a proud symbol for Canadian youth.
Even after his death, Mr. Speaker, Victor Davis continued to set an example by donating his vital organs, his heart, eyes, lungs, liver and kidneys, so that other persons may live.
His fighting spirit and his love and respect for his fellow men were qualities that endeared him to all Canadians and won him their respect, admiration and love.
I wish to extend our condolences and express our feelings of sympathy and profound sadness to all members of his family.
Victor Davis' example will be with us forever.

Mr. Speaker, President George Bush has defended U.S. military aid to the government in El Salvador by stating that "Cristiani is doing a job for democracy". "Doing a job for democracy" means the brutal murder of Jesuit priests, the detention of foreign nationals and terrorizing of the civilian population. Increased militarization will not lead to democratization as the United States maintains.
Bush argues that the elections in El Salvador this spring were "certifiably free and fair". Is the U.S. now issuing certificates to justify military intervention? I was in El Salvador at the time of the elections with the Mission for Peace. Our report made clear that elections

Tributes
are only one instrument of a democratic system. If other instruments are absent or weak, elections have questionable validity.
To declare the process in El Salvador fair and free is to severely distort reality. By not formally denouncing the position of the United States, this government is allowing the myth of democracy in El Salvador to be continued. Until the Bush administration accepts that democracy means the participation of all members of society without fear, there will be no peace and no democracy in El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government realizes it is necessary to make youth aware of the dangers of drug abuse and has therefore announced that the week from November 19 to November 25 will be national drug addiction awareness week.
Canada's decision to set up a national anti-drug strategy, initiated in 1987 with a budget of $210 million, is praiseworthy, but drug awareness and prevention programs will not stop the supply of drugs and the dependency it generates.
Today more than ever before, we must be concerned about the insidious effects of drugs.
Increased drug use is a new threat to national security. Life loses its value, the crime rate soars and young people's lives are ruined for good.
Every year, hundreds of millions of dollars worth of drug trafficking profits cross the border between Canada and the United States.
The fight against drugs cannot be won by governments alone. Mr. Speaker, we should take advantage of this week to maximize our efforts to fight drug abuse.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to mourn the death of Lebanese President Rene Mouawad today in Beirut. Mr. Mouawad was elected only a few weeks ago, but already, thanks to his reputation as a man of dialogue, his country was able to move significantly towards peace and national reconciliation, in a land tom by more than 14 years of pitting brother against brother. Canadians welcomed his arrival among the world's heads of state because it
November 22, 1989

marked an important step on the road to the unity, sovereignty and reconstruction of Lebanon.
The attack which took President Mouawad's life is totally unjustifiable and those responsible have dealt Lebanon a heavy blow. The Canadian Government condemns this act and hopes that all parties with influence in Lebanon will show restraint and continue to work towards a political settlement of the Lebanese conflict. Mr. Speaker, violence cannot solve this conflict.
President Mouawad sacrificed himself to make the Lebanese nation what it was before, a beacon of civilization and community understanding. I wish to express our condolences to President Mouawad's family and to all the people of Lebanon.

Mr. Speaker, the Lebanese community around the world was horrified and shocked at the assassination of President Mouawad early today, an assassination which was undoubtedly a vicious attempt to thwart the Arab League Peace Plan that recently became the only hope of reconciliation to the people of Lebanon and to others around the world.
President Mouawad was elected on November 5 of this year by Lebanese legislators at a special session called for in the peace plan as an attempt to bring to an end 14 years of violence and bloodshed.
I want to call on the Arab League to not be discouraged by this brutal act, to not let this act deter them in their efforts toward a final resolution of this long and tragic conflict, and to elect another president quickly to avoid any further deterioration that would almost undoubtedly result in absolute anarchy.
I want to call on General Aoun to endorse the peace plan by offering full support to the process and decisions agreed upon by the Lebanese legislators and the Arab League.
I want to call on the Government of Canada, this time to use our seat on the Security Council, bring the matter up for action and show the people of Lebanon that we will not stand by any more while innocent people are being murdered, and that we will be willing to work with them, to work with the Arab League, to put an end, once
Oral Questions
and for all, to this senseless killing that is tearing the heart out of the Middle East.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party I would like to join with everyone here in the House of Commons in condemning this act of violence, the assassination of the President of Lebanon.
We extend our sympathies not only to the family of the president but to the entire people of Lebanon who have suffered these last 14 years an endless cycle of violence which can only be perpetuated by the kind of violence which we saw enacted there today in the bombing that killed the president.
I am reminded that today is the anniversary of another assassination, the assassination of President Kennedy on November 22,1963. We see that whatever hopes that we had at that time that assassination might disappear from the face of the earth have been shattered time and time again and are shattered here today, shattered in a country where assassination and violence have become a way of life.
I join in the appeal that the Arab League and others who are sincere about peace in Lebanon not be discouraged by this event, that the life and the courage of the President of Lebanon, who no doubt knew that this was a dangerous job when he took it on, not be offered up in vain, and that some day soon everyone who has influence and power in that region of the world will come to their senses and make it possible for peace to come to the people of Lebanon.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the position of the government and the position that we have taken as a party for many, many years is that we will honour the type of marketing system that producers want. If the majority of producers want a marketing board system, that is something we will facilitate for them. The fact of the matter is that-
Did you check the free trade agreement?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a Liberal is saying from her seat that that is not what the free trade agreement says. The free trade agreement veiy clearly establishes the right for marketing boards to exist under the provisions of GATT.
What this government is doing during the GATT negotiations is an attempt to clarify and strengthen Article 11, the foundation under which supply management systems can exist and under which import controls can be implemented.
As a result of the ice cream and yoghurt decision, which was not a free trade decision but rather a GATT decision, it is necessary to clarify that provision because the wording goes back to 1947 and there have been a lot of changes since that time.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister might focus on answering the question. All sides of the House applauded when east bloc countries, specifically East Germany, began tearing down the wall that kept people in. Now East Germans have a choice.
Will the minister and his government tear down the blockage that exists in the natural products marketing law which restricts the producers of grains and oilseeds, livestock, fruits and vegetables from even considering establishing such marketing boards? They have to get the legislation changed first. They have to get permission to go through the wall. Will he tear it down?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has been living in Ottawa too long and not getting back to his constituency often enough.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If he was paying any attention to what was going on in rural Canada, he would know that beef producers in Ontario rejected a marketing board and supply management concept.
We believe in democracy. If they had voted in favour of one, we probably would have taken action to facilitate that course, but democratic forces prevailed. They did not want that kind of a system, and we will uphold the decision of the farmers.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance.
After a convention of North American chiefs of police held recently in Kentucky in the United States it would seem that billions of dollars of drug trafficking profits cross the American border every year and are laundered in Canadian financial institutions.
Considering that the laws of our two countries are not compatible and that our banks can break up a large deposit into several smaller deposits to various bank accounts and then transfer them to U.S. accounts, with a view to correcting this situation, does the minister intend to take appropriate and concrete steps to authorize our police forces to obtain information from our banking institutions so as to uncover these fraudulent operations
November 22, 1989

and enable our society to make progress in the fight against drugs?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government looks upon money laundering as a serious issue. I should like to reassure the Hon. member for Drummond by telling him that we have been and will be using the latest and most effective measures to fight against this plague.
For example, some people have suggested registering any transaction in excess of $10,000. My response is that drug traffickers may be criminals, but they are not necessarily stupid. It is very easy to find other ways to complete the transaction. We looked at that suggestion on three occasions and, for the time being, our conclusion is that the methods we use with the banks, the RCMP and the Superintendent of Financial Institutions are up to date and effective. We will continue to use the latest technology.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State (Agriculture).
Yesterday, while some 15,000 angry farmers were protesting-
Oh, oh!

The minister had the gall to brag in the House about his dairy policy. Is the minister not aware that his policy became worthless when his government signed a free-trade agreement with the United States, and especially decided to progressively remove the tariff on yogurt and ice cream, before securing from the United States the assurance that they would allow Canada to add these two items to its import control list? Does the minister not realize that the people who were outside booing him and insisting they no longer trusted him are seeking a better treatment from him? What is he going to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realized that I was fortunate to hold two portfolios when RCMP officers advised me that there were 4,500 farm producers demonstrating yesterday in front of Parliament.
Oral Questions
In this connection, my Hon. friend ought to know that the decision dealing with yogurt and ice cream-
I am aware that NDP members could not care less about Quebec farm producers, but I suggest that there are people both in and out of the House who care about them.
In reply to his question, may I suggest to my Hon. friend that he should know this is a GATT decision which has nothing to do with our free trade agreement with the United States. It was at the request of farm producers that we had added yogurt and ice cream to that list. The tribunal ruled against us; yet, we have done something which Liberal Governments had not done in over 20 years, to wit, sit down with Quebec farm producers in an effort to put together a new dairy policy and strategy with respect to GATT talks. You did not even have a long-term dairy policy. For five years, farm producers waited for some action on your part.
Since my colleague is absent from the House, may I suggest, as I did yesterday, that we have no lesson to receive from hon. members opposite. We have always looked after dairy producers and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Minister of State (Agriculture), who is fully aware that he simply extended for a five-year period a dairy policy that has been of benefit to Quebec farmers for years and years as it was renewed by the Liberal administration. The industrial milk policy has done so well in Quebec because it was well designed years ago.
When in 1976 there were demonstrations on Parliament Hill, the government of the day listened and made corrections.
Here is my question to the minister: Faced with that demonstration, by whatever the number of farmers, because all farmers in UPA and the whole UPA membership in the province of Quebec, support those who came to Parliament Hill and are demanding that the Minister take concrete steps to protect, not only yogurt and ice cream, but also butter, cheese, powdered milk.
What will the minister do to ensure that Canada's industrial milk producers are not put out of business by the Americans, as they are now preparing to do?

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is amazing that after five years the hon. member for Papineau would ask a question dealing with agriculture. For five years, Mr. Speaker, this government has been looking after farmers. In 1986 we brought in the first long-term dairy policy ever a policy they could not get from you.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, which is of significant importance for dairy farmers, they sit with us on a strategy committee. We are reviewing the current dairy policy with a view to strengthening it and ensuring-
Order!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
If you will listen-and ensuring that we are able not only to address what we have gone through over the last three years, but also to meet the challenges of the future.
We believe that under a strengthened and clarified Article 11 marketing boards will be in a position to compete during the 1990s and into the next century, Mr. Speaker. This is what farmers need.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans who has thrown in the towel in determining fishery policy in Atlantic Canada, leaving two big fish companies to call the shots on which fish plants to close and leaving thousands of plant workers and fishermen economically stranded.
Does the minister not agree that catch quotas rightfully belong to the individual ports and fish plants, and not to the companies?
If the companies tty to close particular plants in Atlantic Canada, will he ensure that the appropriate quota shares remain with the individual fish plants? Does he not agree that sharing the work is better than shutting down individual plants altogether, permanently?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the hon. member that I certainly have not agreed to throw in the towel, although if he needs one, feeling rather wet, I could provide him with one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Actually it is a crying towel.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are certain matters with respect to the distribution of fish quotas that come ultimately under the authority of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
As we plan for the quota management of the 1990 fishery we will be setting those quotas in a fair and equitable fashion, following a process of consultation involving all industry sector groups, affected provincial governments and ministers of fisheries.
There are other matters as to which plants should receive which portion of supply under quotas accorded to private companies which have been properly the domain of those private companies. In the course of the work of the special cabinet committee on the northern cod issue in particular and the Atlantic fishery more generally, that matter is being considered very carefully.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows as much about towels as he does about the fishery.
Does he not agree that the fish belong to the communities and the people, not to those multinational fish companies?
Yesterday there were some meetings in Halifax on this subject. I am sure the minister has heard reports are circulating from that meeting yesterday that both inshore and offshore quotas are going to be drastically reduced. That should come as no surprise to him.
Will the minister now bite the bullet and set some direction on how the quotas are to be distributed between the offshore and the inshore? Will he undertake to see that the two sectors of the industry are not being played off one against the other, leaving the industry in even deeper chaos?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first the member was concerned that I would throw in the towel. Now he wants me to bite the bullet. I think he really needs a shot in the arm.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
The hon. member knows full well that for several years there has been a process of consultation in which we discuss these questions with the affected sectors of the Atlantic fishing industry and provincial governments.
November 22, 1989

Upon completion of that process of consultation we will publish the 1990 Atlantic Groundfish Management Plan on or around December 30 or 31 of this year, and all the answers to his questions will be revealed at that time.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. The minister will know that the Prime Minister said yesterday in Moscow that the 1987 White Paper on Defence was outdated. Of course the Prime Minister was the last person in Canada to realize this, but we are glad he has come to this conclusion.
I am wondering if the Minister of National Defence could tell us what process the government now has in mind for reconstructing Canadian defence policy along the lines of the new realities that the Prime Minister has observed, and whether in the context of that process he is prepared to say now that the government will suspend its commitment to low-level flight testing over Innu territory in Labrador until such time as the government can arrive at a new defence policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member asks a very important question. The White Paper was drafted in 1985 to 1987. It was released in 1987 and it was the reality of the time. I think the hon. member admits that, as do others.
Several things have happened since that White Paper was drafted. There was a budget and, to provide the economy of Canada with the strength that we think it needs, there was a reduction in the allocation for the Department of National Defence. A review was undertaken at that time and it is still ongoing.
There are realities today and there are opportunities today that were not available four weeks ago and were not available some six months ago. Therefore, naturally we look at the changes as we progress and the White Paper will continue to be reviewed.
I suggest to the hon. member that it would be prudent to take the time and to allow this government to take the time to come to the right answers as there is a changing reality in the world today.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, with respect, I think the minister should acknowledge that even in 1987 there was disagreement about the White Paper. It is true, of course, that other things have happened in the meantime.
I asked the minister about a process for reviewing the White Paper, and I asked him in that context to suspend the government's commitment to low-level flight testing, to put a moratorium on it until such time as it can be re-evaluated. The minister has not answered that question.
In the same context, would he also consider suspending Canada's commitment to cruise missile testing which also belongs to a very outdated view of the world?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member represents a party which believes we should not seek collective security in the NATO alliance. This government believes we should and that we should continue to seek security in the NATO alliance.
The member has to understand, and I am sure he does. The changes that have been taking place in Europe today, yesterday and the day before were changes that were encouraged by NATO over the whole period of its existence. NATO has never been an aggressive force. NATO has been a defensive force. It will continue to be. So are the activities and the training that Canada takes part in today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to advise that in view of the intervention of the hon. minister and the replies by the opposition parties, we will end Question Period at 3.05.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
My question is for the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. In February the minister and Investment Canada approved the takeover of Texaco by Imperial Oil even though the Investment Canada Act says that the question of competition must be resolved first, and that was not done until June. Even though the question of competition was resolved in June, the competition tribunal said that the decision on competition was flawed on November 10.

November 22, 1989
Oral Questions
If the competition question was not resolved until November 10, how could Investment Canada give its approval and say that the competition question was resolved in February, thereby violating its own enabling legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mandate of Investment Canada was to examine mergers and acquisitions to see if they are in the national interest. In matters relating to the oil and gas industry, it is the oil and gas policy that imposes certain restraints and applies particularly to upstream assets, namely the oil and gas in-ground reserves.
Those policy requirements were met in terms of this agreement. There were certain dispersals imposed on Imperial Oil. It had to dispose of certain assets and so on in order to meet the requirements of the energy policy.
The Competition Act has its own authority and there is no sequential arrangement. They both must be approved before any acquisition is finally approved. As you know, the competition questions are currently being examined very closely and certain amendments being caused, and that will carry itself to its conclusion. Either it will be permitted or not permitted, but that has nothing to do with Investment Canada's responsibility and mandate.

Mr. Speaker, yes it does, because the Investment Canada Act says that the question of competition must be resolved before Investment Canada can give its approval to the takeover, and it did not do that. In fact, the competition question was not resolved until four months after Investment Canada gave its approval.
From here on, will Investment Canada wait until the competition question is resolved before giving its approval on investments such as this, particularly takeovers and mergers, or is this going to be a regular procedure, that of the enabling legislation of Investment Canada being breached for the convenience of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not for the convenience of the government, it is for the convenience of commerce in the country. I do not see any advantage to anybody to follow the procedure the hon. member is suggesting. There are two conditions that must be met; the net benefit to Canada test of Investment Canada and
the Competition Act test. Each must be met separately or a deal does not go through. The procedure the hon. member seems to be suggesting offers no benefits to anybody.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. He will know that the United Nations General Assembly has approved a comprehensive convention with regard to the rights of the child. Canadian governments, both present and past, have been strong advocates of this. Today 10 per cent of Canadian children are in need of some form of child care, however, they are not being accommodated. In Ontario 11 per cent of the province's children in need are being served by the child care program in this country.
Why is the government of Canada not finding this subject matter to be sufficiently important to introduce a comprehensive program, thereby creating the many new spaces which are needed for child care in this country? Is it or is it not a priority?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member knows that this was the first government in Canada that did try to introduce a comprehensive child care plan for children in Canada and that it was stopped by the other place with his party being instrumental in that stoppage.
Let me say as well that this government has committed itself to bringing in another comprehensive child care plan before the next election, within the next two or three years, and that in the meantime the Canada Assistance Plan is available for the provinces to use. It is an open-ended plan to which this government is committed.

The minister knows that they have had almost six years to come forward with a national program for child care and they have failed with that particular priority.
There are fewer than 70 child care centres serving more than 1,000 native communities across Canada, some of which are now facing closure because of lack of
November 22, 1989

funds. At the present time the Government of Canada spends less than $5 million for First Nation child care.
Would the minister explain why the government has gutted $60 million from native child care? Why is the Government of Canada denying native people, whose needs must be obvious to everyone in this House, of high quality and culturally sensitive child care?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government is well aware of the particular needs of native children and of native women. We have done more to show that than has any previous government. Let me go back to some other things too.
In terms of child care, this government introduced tax measures that will provide financial assistance to parents. We launched the Child Care Initiative Fund which includes the very kinds of things the hon. member is talking about. The Child Care Initiative Fund was set up specifically to deal with doubly disadvantaged children and women who need particular help, such as native inamen. That is in action now and it is moving forward. This government also recognizes that we need to have a national child care program and we will do that as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today on a question of privilege. My background is Italian, and my office received an anonymous telephone call asking whether that made me a mafioso. Enquiries were made, and it seems that Tele-Direct, the company responsible for printing the yellow pages across Canada, has committed a grave injustice vis-a-vis the Italian-Canadian community. College Platon, established in 1957, is a language school and teaches 25 different languages. The college is located in Montreal and is known not only to Canadians but also to foreign students. For the year 1990-91, the college placed an ad in the yellow pages on page 453, listing 23 courses offered to students. It says: "English, French, Portuguese, Dutch", and so forth, but instead of Italian, it says: "mafia".
Point of Order
Needless to say, the entire Italian-Canadian community, of which I am a member, was shocked by this racial slur. When Italians first immigrated to Canada, Mr. Speaker, they were called a number of unpleasant names like "mafioso". We worked as labourers for abysmally low wages, to gain recognition and be accepted as solid citizens. For 20 years we have been part of the Canadian and Quebec community.
Just look at the newspapers! Italians are no more likely than the English, French or dyed-in-the-wool Quebecers to commit crimes, rape, or be involved in shady dealings or drugs. We are Canadians, not mafiosi. On behalf of the Italian-Canadian community I represent, I ask Tele-Direct to take action against the person or persons with this warped attitude and withdraw this racist page from the directories or make the appropriate corrections.
Mr. Speaker, the Italian community doesn't deserve to be treated like this in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I listened with some interest to the hon. member's statement. This is a veiy serious matter. It may be appropriate for the Chair to consider the matter and make a statement later on in the House. I want to thank the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, although I have not seen the document, I agree with the hon. member that in 1989, such insults are unacceptable, and speaking on behalf of the Italian community and with the hon. member, I hope that with the support of this House, steps will be taken to prevent any recurrences.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief point of order arising from the proceedings during Question Period yesterday, November 21. This is the first opportunity I have had to raise the point.
It has to do with a question put by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell who said, as reported at pages 5931 and 5932 of Hansard:

November 22, 1989
Point of Order
Given that less than four hours later Radio-Canada confirmed that the Federal Business Development Bank had made two loans to the Lido strip joint in Hull owned and operated by a friend of a former cabinet minister and totalling $1.3 million -
Mr. Speaker, I have heard you many times in this House, indeed I heard you today and yesterday, admonish members about using preambles and comments that amount to charges or impugned motives and so on. No doubt you are reflecting the admonitions in Beau-chesne's sixth edition, section 409(7) which says:
A question must adhere to the proprieties of the House, in terms of inferences, imputing motives or casting aspersions upon persons within the House or out of it.
In this particular case the reference is to a former cabinet minister, with the inference that somehow perhaps he influenced this loan which I admitted was an error.
Outside the House the hon. member mentioned that it was Roch LaSalle he was talking about. That, of course, had the press going and they were pursuing me to see if I was going to follow this up with a full investigation into what was to them imputed wrong-doing. Other reporters checked that out and Mr. LaSalle denied categorically knowing the owners of the Lido strip joint or ever having been in the establishment. My office confirmed that. He absolutely denies that.
Mr. Speaker, in keeping with your admonitions my request is veiy simple. I am not accusing the hon. member of deliberately inferring wrong-doing on the part of Mr. LaSalle. He may have received information which was in error.
In any event, I think it would be in keeping with the kind of atmosphere we would like to promote in this House if the hon. member would withdraw that comment and recognize that Mr. LaSalle is not a friend of the owner of this strip joint and has not been a frequenter of this strip joint. He should recognize that any reflection such as that is unfair to this person who is no longer a member of this House, and particularly unfair to that person's family.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I invite you to read carefully what Hansard says and what the minister himself has stated:
-four hours later Radio-Canada confirmed that the Federal Business Development Bank had made two loans to the Lido strip joint in Hull owned and operated by a friend of a former cabinet minister-
I was stating what Radio-Canada had said. If the minister across has some difficulty with what reporters of Radio-Canada say, he can phone Mr. Normand Lester at Radio-Canada and ask him publicly to recant.
As you will know, Mr. Speaker, neither members of the opposition nor anyone else in this House are in a position to dictate to Radio-Canada what to say. I would imagine that Mr. Normand Lester has a mind of his own, he can say what he likes, and if that is not satisfactory to either Mr. LaSalle or to someone else they can take it up with Mr. Lester or with Stevie Cameron or all the others who have made such statements. But for me to read what has been said on television last night can hardly be considered a slander or anything of the like, and I say to the minister across the way that just because he does not like something does not make it slanderous.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will consider the interventions that have been made and report back to the House.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order. If I am not mistaken, the hon. minister who raised the point of order was in the House yesterday at the time that the words he complains of were spoken by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. He heard the words and he therefore was in the position to raise the point of order, if one existed, promptly after yesterday's Question Period.
I just point out he did not do so at the first opportunity. I simply add that point to what I think are the extremely valid words of the member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, and I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that words like those used by the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell citing basically a press report have been used many times in this House by members on the government side when they were in opposition and in replying to questions and no complaint has been made. I think there is no validity, as a result, to what was said by the hon. minister in his point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time the accusation was made by way of statement, I had no way of knowing if it was true or not true. Of course, no names were given at that time. It was outside the House that the name Roch LaSalle was mentioned so I did not have the opportunity to verify. I then sought out independent verification. My office talked to Roch LaSalle and he is again deploring the fact that even though he has left this place, his family continues to be abused in this fashion. It is for that reason and that reason alone that I just say,
November 22, 1989

Routine Proceedings

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
would it not be nice if for once we could say, "We are sorry we dragged your name through this muddy situation, it should not have been dragged through".
I did not suggest the hon. member invented this fact. He says he got it from Radio-Canada, that is fine. However, is it not about time that perhaps just out of decency, out of respect for the man's family, we acknowledge a mistake was made and withdraw the remark. That is all I was asking for, Herb, that is all I wanted.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic

speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill C-278, an act respecting compensation for Canadian victims of crime travelling or posted abroad.

November 22, 1989
Routine Proceedings

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is it the
pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to introduce the bill?
Agreed.

Madam Speaker, this bill is designed to fill a gap in compensation for criminal injuries. All provinces and territories in Canada have legislation under which victims of criminal acts have an opportunity to apply for compensation from the province. Unfortunately, if a Canadian is travelling or working abroad and is injured there is no possibility of claiming compensation. The event must occur within the provincial or territorial jurisdiction.
This bill is designed to provide, at the federal level, that Canadians who are travelling or working abroad and are injured may apply to their provincial or territorial compensation tribunals and would assume that the federal government would pick up the compensation thus applied for.
I urge the House, at the appropriate time, to adopt the legislation.
