speechtext: The House resumed from Thesday, November 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lewis that Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to speak on this bill, although it is a very difficult matter. It is the act respecting abortion, Bill C-43.
I believe the bill is unfortunately mistaken. It is no doubt well meant, but I believe if it were enacted it would do more harm than good. Therefore, I must oppose it.
In brief, the bill tries to outlaw abortion by using the Criminal Code and the threat of prison, but then it goes on to try to excuse abortion in most of those cases.
What is the effect? The effect will be confusion. It will be to make a number of women and doctors fearful, perhaps with cause, that is, that they might be imprisoned, perhaps without cause. The results in the courts will be uncertain. It will worsen conditions for normal childbirth; and it will not reduce the number of abortions.
It is the wrong way to go. It is impractical. There is no need to recriminalize abortion.
The problem of which abortions are very often the expression is a problem of family life. We should rather be looking at the causes of family trouble.
In fact, it is my understanding that abortion from a moral standpoint may be murder of a person, as some people are pointing out in this debate, but that from a legal standpoint the comparison with murder is mistaken. The reason is that the foetus is inside another person. Even if the foetus be regarded as a person still the fact is unchanged that it is inside another person. We cannot separate them to protect one or both separately.

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
I want to remind the House of part of the opinion given by Chief Justice Brian Dickson of the Supreme Court of Canada who said:
Forcing a woman, by threat of criminal sanction, to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations, is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus a violation of security of the person.
In the same court Madam Justice Bertha Wilson said:
Liberty in a free and democratic society does not require the state to approve the personal decisions made by its citizens; it does, however, require the state to respect them.
I believe along with her that this is a personal decision in which there is indeed a moral obligation. There may be several moral obligations. They may even seem to be in conflict with each other. The state does not have a duty to agree with this decision or that decision in that case but it does have a duty to respect the decision.
She goes on to state:
It is a decision that deeply reflects the way the woman thinks about herself and her relationship to others and to society at large. It is not just a medical decision; it is a profound social and ethical one as well. Her response to it will be the response of the whole person.
In other words, it is not a private, individual or isolated act. It is the act of a person who is a member of society and who normally recognizes that membership. It seems to me that there is a tendency among some of the remarks I have heard in this debate to regard women in a traditional way as somehow weaker. Not only weaker in body, but weaker in moral fibre. I do not know any good reason for holding that view. We do not assume that about men in that case, although there could be an argument for saying that generally women exercise more responsibility about childbirth than men do. In a country where most of the police are men, most of the lawyers are men, most of the judges are men, most of the legislators are men, it is a little disturbing to hear again and again the suggestion that a woman is not fit to make this moral decision.
The fact is that there are countries that have taken the line that some people here would like them to take, countries such as Brazil, Ireland, Italy and Romania.
They all have very severe laws against abortion. They all have a much higher rate of abortion than Canada does.
It seems foolish to repeat their experience by insisting on an extreme law, an extreme threat of punishment in the matter of abortion. In Brazil, there are 4 million abortions annually where there are 3 million live births. That is a dreadful situation, but it is not stopped by criminal threats. In Romania, I read in The Toronto Star, the birthrate there has dropped from 24 births per thousand women in the late 1940s to 14 per thousand in our time. This is in spite of a very severe prohibition and threat of punishment for abortion. In fact abortion deaths there have soared from about 25 per million women in the year before the present government to about 100 per million-four times the amount in the 1980s.
There seems no good reason among those who have spoken for recriminalizing abortion. In fact, it is not even clear that there is any reason to change the status since the Morgentaler decision.
Planned Parenthood has pointed out that abortions have not increased since the Supreme Court of Canada ruling in January, 1988. That is in its report from which I have just quoted.
The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada does not feel that the situation is out of hand because we lack specific criminal prohibition of abortion. The society points this out in its official statement entitled, the "SOGC Abortion Position",
To circumvent the need for abortion should always be the ultimate goal. To this end, there is great value and urgency for provincial Ministers of Health, Education and Social and Community Services to integrate programs devoted to sex education with family planning clinics and abortion services. Only in this way can the adolescent population that contributes so heavily to the abortion statistics be reached effectively.
They also point out that the decision to perform an abortion should be considered a medical one and as such the issue of therapeutic abortions should be removed from Canadian criminal law.
This is the opinion of the specialists in this subject. They go on to state:
Nevertheless, abortion services should be uniformly available to women across Canada.
Of course this law does absolutely nothing to bring that about.
November 22, 1989

The Canadian Medical Association has also issued its statement in the matter in which, in part, it states:
The decision to perform an induced abortion is a medical one made confidentially-
That is an important point, Madam Speaker.
-between the patient and her physician within the confines of existing Canadian law. The decision is made after conscientious examination of all other options.
The proposed bill is rather insulting to all these medical doctors by suggesting that they are not now exercising their professional responsibility in the matter.
Induced abortion requires medical and surgical expertise and is a medical act. It should be performed only in a facility that meets approved medical standards, not necessarily a hospital.
The argument some people have used is that there are a growing number of abortions. Certainly I, for one, am not happy with the number of abortions, or even with any abortions. My wife and I, as we have had opportunity, have occasionally been able to encourage and help a person to choose a course of action other than abortion, but it was her choice.
The statistics are interesting. In 1970 there were 11,200 abortions in Canada. In 1982, there were 66,319, a large increase. But in 1987, there were 63,662, almost 3,000 less abortions five years later. There has not been an explosion of abortions.
If you look at how many abortions are performed per thousand women, again the number rose 2.5 per thousand women in 1970. In 1982 it was 11.1 per thousand women; and then it dropped in 1987 to 10.2 per thousand women.
It is interesting if you look at the ratio of abortions per hundred to live births to see how many abortions there were. It went from three in 1970 to 17.8 in 1982, again a large increase. It then dropped a small amount to 17.2 in 1987. Abortions peaked in 1982 and have been declining since then. That is true of the number of abortions per woman and the number of abortions per live births, although they declined less.
I think the explanation is in the live birth rate, not in the abortion rate. In 1970 there were 371,988 live births. In 1982, 12 years later with a larger population, there were 372,882, only 900 more, a very tiny increase of live
Government Orders
births. In 1987, there were 372,080; in other words, a drop of 800 live births between 1982 and 1987, a time when there was a drop of 3,000 in the number of abortions.
The problem is not with abortions. When the population has gone up by 20 per cent, obviously the number of women has increased. The proportion of abortions to women has gone down slightly. The proportion of abortions to live births has gone down slightly more. The problem is not with abortions but with the country's fertility rate; that is to say from the point of view of those who worry about the number of live births. I do not worry about it personally. Alice and I have seven children and 13 grandchildren and we are hoping for more grandchildren.
Those who talk about the rate of abortions imply that somehow or other it is a cause in itself of all these troubles. That is simply not true. It is much more a result of the breakdown of family life: the rate of divorce, the rate of separation and the large number of single parents, mostly women. These are very much concerns of the last 20 and 30 years. To pin them all down to abortion would be to stand the matter on its head. Other speakers have pointed out, including the last speaker last night, Mrs. Bertrand, that we should be looking at the sources of family trouble. I find those sources largely in a market-driven economy. Children are treated as unproductive or at least unprofitable. In other words, we seem to be sliding back to the days when governments in England in the last century had to legislate that it was not allowable to cause children under 10 years of age to work in the mines. The issue of child labour, or the proposal of child labour, has only been advocated by a few groups like the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. It is not a serious threat yet.
What is a serious threat is the refusal of those who build our cities and housing to provide room physically for children. In Toronto, between 1951 and 1971 there was a net loss of about 20,000 units that had two bedrooms. There are other characteristics of family units but that is a basic one. Just recently, between 1976 and 1985, in the new building with demolition subtracted-in other words, the net increase of residential units-the units that were suitable for families in 1976 were 32.4 per cent of the whole. They declined from there so that the

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
average now is that family units are only 17.5 per cent of the total units of housing being built in the city of Toronto.
Of course, the builders argued that it was the market which wants that. In fact, I have many people coming to me now, as they came when I was an alderman in the centre of the city, complaining about not being able to find a place for children. In the 1970s it was landlords who explicitly and openly forbade children in their apartments which is now, fortunately, illegal.
In the city of Toronto in 1971, there were 28.6 children for every 100 adults and in 1986 there were only 20.5. In other words, there has been a drop from 28.6 to 20.5 in 15 years in the percentage of children to adults.
In Toronto, children are hungry. According to the Daily Bread Food Bank survey, an estimated 72,000 children 17 years of age and under in metro have found it necessary to use a food program on an average of three times in the past year. Of families using food assistance, I quote: "Sixty-five per cent are single-parent families; 15 per cent of all metro families are single-parent families, but 65 per cent use the food banks". Again I quote: "Children nine years of age or younger are 11.3 per cent of the population of metro but 28.3 per cent of the food bank population". In other words, children of nine years of age have an almost three times greater chance of being forced to go to the food banks.
Those figures from the Daily Bread Food Bank relate to the people who have come to my office because they cannot find a place to live where they can pay rent and still have money for food for themselves and their children. This is a very serious problem in family life in our cities. No wonder there are strains, wife beatings, child beatings, break-up of families when it is impossible to find a place to live without moving right out of the city, when it is impossible to find a place to work since Toronto has a high level of unemployment, even if you do not count the 10,000 or 20,000 people who are homeless because nobody can survey them to find out whether they were looking for work last week.
It goes further than that. There are many ways in which the economy of this country, which finds children unprofitable and therefore considers them really unproductive, simply prices children not only out of the city but out of a decent chance to live. It is very often the mothers of those children who decide that they will make
a dreadful decision to avoid having more children that they cannot feed.
My points are that the bill is mistaken. It will not work. My point is that it is ethically wrong to confuse a moral decision and a moral responsibility with a legal responsibility. My point is there is no occasion for recriminalizing abortion because the medical profession has it properly in hand. There is no crisis of increased abortion. There is a crisis of family life. Therefore, this bill should be scrapped and the government should get to work with some of its promises to provide for day care and the other things that a family needs.

Madam Speaker, I enjoyed the debate of the hon. member from Spadina. I would like at the outset to indicate that contrary to his suggestion that because abortion is a moral issue, therefore there ought to be no law on it, I would like to remind the hon. member that in the history of legal construction, the foundation of a good law in fact is morality.
My questions for the hon. member are: first, would he agree that where there are no genuine reasons to do an abortion he would respect the decision of the physician, rather than just asking whether there be no medical reasons not to have an abortion, as his leader said yesterday? There is a great deal of difference between the two positions.
It is the tradition of medical practice, as a medical doctor by background, that before a physician does a medical procedure or prescribes therapy, there ought to exist a rationale for treatment. It is not enough only to say that there does not exist a contraindication for such a treatment. That is only one of the factors when a physician prescribes a therapy.
My second question for the hon. member is: would he agree that when a medical doctor says that there exists no indication for abortion he would respect not only the decision of that medical doctor but also to require that the decision ought to be based only on the basis that there is a threat to the life of the pregnant mother.

Madam Speaker, in reply to the hon. member's first point, I would say that while law should be based on moral considerations, not by any means every moral consideration ought to be made the subject of a law. There are many moral considerations which must be left to individuals singly or in groups to work out among themselves. This is one of them.

Second, the position that I have taken, and for that matter my leader has taken, and that the Medical Association and the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists has taken is not the position that the hon. member has suggested. They are not saying they will do an abortion only when they find medical grounds. What they have said is abortion should not be regulated in the Criminal Code. They would want to make sure that the abortion was done under appropriate conditions. They have not defined the conditions in the statements that I have referred to because we have recognized in our law, including the criminal law, that the doctor has the responsibility for judging those conditions. That is not to say that they will judge them only on medical grounds.
Poverty may not be a medical matter but it has medical consequences. For example, it has been found in Montreal that children born of mothers who have been malnourished are almost certainly doomed to an unhealthy life. That is the kind of thing that a doctor may recognize even though it is not necessarily the subject of a medical decision.
The point I am making is the reasons for abortion. The reasons why in fact women have chosen abortion and will continue to choose abortion regardless of what the hon. member may wish, regardless of what I may wish, are social and economic. They have to do with the fact that a great many mothers now must work; with the fact that a great many fathers now do not want to support their children or do it badly. Those are the sorts of facts that move many women to seek an abortion. They are not a matter for a medical judgment but they are a matter for medical care by a qualified practitioner. That is the point that the Medical Association has made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just briefly, I would like to make some comments on the whole subject of criminalization in relation to abortion because I have heard the pleas of the member for Trinity-Spadina and his complaint that he does not want to see abortion criminalized. That notion is unwarranted, given the state of law in Canada.
Government Orders
The Parliament of Canada has only one basis for legislating with respect to abortion and that is the criminal law power. There is no other way the Parliament of Canada can legislate with respect to abortion unless it exercises its power to enact criminal law. It is only in that academic sense that Parliament is criminalizing abortion.
The whole fact of the matter is that if there is to be a prohibition, there must be a sanction, there must be a penalty and that can be called criminal law. Whether the province enacts legislation dealing with abortion, as has happened in my province of Nova Scotia restricting the place at which abortions can be performed, or whether the Parliament of Canada enacts a prohibition, it must be enforced by a penalty and that is what we call criminal law.
The question is not really criminalizing abortion, the question is: are we going to legislate with respect to abortion? I hope the member will understand that because his or her choice, as a member of Parliament, is to vote against the law, whether they characterize it as criminal or some other kind of a law.
The real question is, and I do not want to see the member avoid it: should Parliament legislate with respect to abortion? That is the issue. Do not be confused by terms like criminalize and so on. Make your decision on that question: should Parliament legislate with respect to abortion? I think that Parliament should legislate with respect to abortion. If the member does not agree with that, he simply votes against it. Do not bring in questions like criminalize or non-criminalize to confuse the issue.

Madam Speaker, I think Parliament should indeed legislate with respect to abortion. I do not share the hon. member's one-eyed vision where he thinks the only thing Parliament can do is to prohibit. Of course, if the member wants to prohibit abortion or if the member wants to prohibit wearing eye glasses or having white hair or anything like that, the only way he can do it is by getting Parliament to put it into the Criminal Code.
I do not want to prohibit abortion. I would like to bring abortions to an end or to a much smaller number. I have spoken before and today on how that should be done. Prohibition is what I said did not work in Ireland, Italy,

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
Brazil, Romania and probably failed to work in many other countries. It is a stupid thing to tty here.
There is legislation that Parliament ought to consider for abortion. It ought to amend the National Health Act to ensure that the basic principle of the National Health Act is upheld across this country and that abortion services are equally available to women in all parts of Canada. That would be parliamentary legislation which would improve the health of all concerned. It would be a step to accompany, for example, legislation, to provide day care services for the children of working mothers which would do more than anything else I can think of to reduce the number of abortions.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-43, legislation that we have introduced to deal with abortion.
Some of my colleagues will know that I have spoken in this House on three previous occasions on the issue of abortion: twice with respect to private members' bills and once last year when we had the debate to determine if there might be a sense of the House about how we might proceed with the issue.
I think my personal views which I have expressed on this issue are well known to members of the Housed believe that women should have the broadest possible range of freedom to make decisions about themselves, their bodies and their futures. Like many of my colleagues, particularly some of my female colleagues who have spoken on this legislation in the past week, I have come to this debate with some concerns, a lot of thought and some heartache but finally in my own mind with a recognition that what we have brought forward is fair and does meet basic criteria which I believe are important for women and is also workable.
I also understand how so many other of my colleagues, who have come to view this issue from a different kind of perspective, have worked hard and how caucus members have worked together to see if there is a way that we can jointly come forward with what the role of the state and the government should be in providing a regime with respect to abortion. Upon reflection, I will be supporting the bill because I think it is fair; I think it is workable.
I would like the opportunity today to go back and look at how I feel and where I have come from on this debate, talk a bit about the legislation and talk a bit in more general terms about the issue of abortion itself. Certainly, in terms of my own thinking this goes back many, many years recognizing that as a woman in modern-day society we have had to fight pretty long and hard to gain legal equality, to gain economic and social equality in many areas.
I suppose that many of us come from the strong feeling that we do not want to see anything or any law which would in any way restrict that freedom that we fought so hard for. If we look at this issue purely from a feminist point of view, we have difficulty accepting any kinds of restrictions in law that might restrict our ability to make a choice as to whether or not we would want to have an abortion or proceed with a pregnancy.
I also think we have to recognize that no rights are absolute in society and that there always has to be a balance. No one of us can do anything that we want at any time, particularly if it is going to interfere with somebody else. The role of the state is to regulate between often conflicting rights, sometimes the rights of the individual versus the rights of a group or between individuals. That is one of our responsibilities as legislators, to try to achieve that balance while minimizing the interference of the state in the lives of Canadian men and women.
When we think of what we are dealing with here, are there reasons why the state should play a role? Why should I, as a woman, accept that someone else can interfere with my decision? I think there are reasons. When we are dealing with the issue of abortion, we are dealing with something that is different, that does reflect on some very important values that we hold as a society. I guess it does come back to the issue of life or the potential of life. I am not the expert. I am not the one who can say when life begins, and I am not even pretending to be able to do that. However, there is within this issue a recognition of that concern and that value.
As a Canadian society we treasure life. It is fundamental to everything we do in this Parliament, everything we try to do as governments to protect life and to prevent people from interfering with other persons' lives. We pass laws that deal with murder, with assault and with interfering with property rights. We also try in every way
November 22, 1989

possible to enhance the quality of people's lives through the economic and social policies that we put forward because we believe that that is fundamentally our responsibility.
Sometimes when we compare our society with other societies around the world we can see some differences. Whether those differences are rooted in philosophical or religious beliefs, I do not think it matters. But, I think it does matter that in Canadian society we do treasure life. If someone is killed in an automobile accident, that is considered a tragedy and we use the force of the law to sanction those who might have caused that. In some other parts of the world that is not necessarily the case. I think that is a value we have to hold very dear.
When we come back to looking at the question of abortion, I think we do have to consider that balance. This is perhaps an area in which the state does have a legitimate role, a role which the Supreme Court of Canada in dealing with the Morgentaler case recognized that there needed to be a balance between the security of the woman and the potential interest of the state in the foetus. I can accept that balance and therefore I can accept at this time in an imperfect society that we have a right and indeed a responsibility to provide a regime, a set of rules, which tell Canadians on what grounds there is a legal entitlement to abortion and provides a national standard.
I have also had the feeling from many women and men that I have talked to across the country who support the right of women to choose and believe that abortion should be a matter of discussion between a woman and a physician that they want to feel that there are some bounds, that there is some sense as a society that we have a regime in which abortion is regulated. I have come after some considerable thought to accept at this point that we can have a law and if we have a law, what criteria in my mind would be most appropriate?
In coming back to my fundamental belief in the rights of women, I would say first of all it should be a law which minimizes the interference with the right of women to make choices about themselves, about their bodies and about their future. It should be the least intrusive, it should be workable and not create impediments in terms of delays as we had under the former law which created impediments that were inappropriate. It should also in
Government Orders
my mind not restrict where, when or how abortions can be performed.
Abortion, I think everyone would agree, requires medical intervention. We do not want women going back to the past when they tried to induce their own abortions. That is not the right thing. It is not condoned in our society. It is not right for women or for their health. We recognize that it requires the intervention of a qualified medical practitioner and in this legislation we have provided for that, which is determined on the basis of provincial legislation which licenses persons as qualified medical practitioners. Therefore, if it does require a medical procedure, does require the intervention of a medical practitioner, I think it would be irresponsible not to recognize, as my colleague across the floor has indicated, a medical practitioner has to play some role. They have to make a professional judgment about the implications of this medical procedure for the woman and that there has been some considered thought in this decision.
In the legislation we have provided for the criteria to be that if the pregnancy would likely hinder the woman's health, with health being defined in a broad context including physical, mental and psychological, it then provides a joint responsibility. A woman herself has to consider, as I believe she should, why she might wish to proceed with an abortion. Also she would have the professional advice of a medical practitioner who might be able to advise her, first of all, given her particular circumstances what the medical implications might be for her health if she proceeded or not. Obviously there are implications both ways when you are dealing with an issue of this nature.
When we look in terms of society at who can share in making this kind of decision, I think it is appropriate that it is a medical practitioner. That does not, in my mind, take away in an unacceptable manner the right of women to make choices but it is a choice in consultation with a medical practitioner.
The legislation does not restrict where abortions may take place. That would be up to provincial governments. On the other hand, as my colleague from Vancouver Centre pointed out last night-and I agree with her because it does confirm abortion as a medical procedure-it gives greater weight to the understanding that as a medical procedure it should be covered by provincial health care plans. If there were not that kind of consideration it might be easier for provinces to say: "It is not a

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
medical procedure. It does not relate to health. Therefore we do not have a responsibility under our health care plan to provide for it". I think it does help in that respect as well.
There were other approaches that we had discussed. In fact, when we had the debate last year, I put forward an amendment to the motion that was being considered which would have introduced a gestational approach and different degrees of intervention and/or sanctions depending upon the stage of pregnancy.
After having thought about this and talked it over with people of a wide variety of opinions and opposing opinions, I am comfortable with the concept that we should not proceed on that basis. I know some of my colleagues would say that that in itself would imply differential values at different stages of pregnancy. I can find that that is distasteful. It is not necessarily sound philosophically or from any particular point of view.
Also the gestational approach implied incorrectly that women would wait until later stages of pregnancy. We all know that that is not correct. Over 99 per cent of abortions are carried out during the earlier stages and, if a woman is going to make the choice, except under the most unusual circumstances that choice will be made as early as possible. With the legislative base we are proposing, I believe that we will ensure and enhance that abortions can be carried out as quickly as possible because the procedures involved are not complicated. It requires the woman to seek the opinion of her doctor and then be able to proceed.
The other issue which many colleagues have talked about in this House and which friends of mine have discussed is why the Criminal Code, I guess because the Criminal Code connotes in our minds something that is wrong. I do not think that is a fair reflection.
The member for Halifax West who just spoke a few moments ago had a more appropriate perception of why it is necessary to use the Criminal Code. If we are to provide a regulatory regime, a national standard with respect to legal entitlement for abortion, there has to be a mechanism. There has to be a power of government to proceed, and that really is the only one that we have at the federal level.
It does not imply in any way that abortions are wrong. All it is saying is that these are the conditions under which women are legally entitled to have an abortion and that under some situations, either if it is not carried out by a medical practitioner or the criteria are not met, it would be considered inappropriate and the sanction of the law would come forward.
It is wrong to say that this legislation criminalizes abortion or criminalizes women who seek abortions. That is not the intent; that is not the purpose of the law. The purpose of the law is to provide an appropriate, fair regime under which abortions in Canada can proceed.
I would like to take a few minutes to talk about the issue of abortion. No one likes it. No one wishes it upon women. In fact, our deepest desire from all parts of the House would be to try to find ways to minimize the reasons for abortion, the reasons why women seek it as an option. We can never hope to minimize that to zero. I certainly have friends who, despite their best efforts with respect to birth control which has failed, find themselves in a situation where either for health reasons or because they do not want to they are unable to proceed with the pregnancy.
There is a lot we can do. As you look at the figures you recognize it is still young women who are seeking abortions. I read in the paper the other day that in Ontario in 1987, 47 per cent of young women between the ages of 15 and 19 sought abortions. In the Ottawa region itself it was higher. It was 62 per cent of young women between the ages of 15 and 19. That is a very sad reflection. There is something wrong there.
About 15 years ago I was living in Sudbury. I wrote and produced a documentary for the local television station on abortion. I called it To Have or Have Not. Those were early days and I believe in Sudbury it was not possible to obtain a legal abortion because of restrictions in the hospital. It was considered quite something to actually have a television show that talked about these issues.
During the course of researching and producing that documentary I met with people from all different sectors-women who had sought abortions and members of the local women's centre which was the only referral agency to assist women in obtaining abortions. They had to go either to other parts of Ontario or to the United States at that point in time.
November 22, 1989

I talked to women who had decided not to proceed with abortions but to put the baby up for adoption, and I also talked to representatives of agencies involved in that area. I talked to young women who had proceeded with the pregnancy, kept the child and as young unmarried mothers were still trying to cope with completing their schooling or finding a way to survive the problems and how they felt about it. It was a very moving experience to go through that process.
What saddened and angered me was that it seemed that all those women were in losing situations. None of those were really the answer. The answer lay in more effective education and action with respect to the prevention of unwanted pregnancies among that age group, and in a willingness to be more open, to talk about women's reproductive capabilities and what is involved in sexual relations between young people, and to try to encourage both young men and women to accept a greater degree of personal responsibility for their behaviour and to truly seek more viable options for women. Certainly at that time-and I do not think it has improved significantly since-the option of the young woman trying to keep a child creates barriers for her which are almost insurmountable in our society.
I was pleased when the Minister of National Health and Welfare spoke on this issue several days ago and announced a number of new initiatives dealing with all those areas-assisting young people in their own reproduction and in education and improving access to adoption. All those are important. It is not something that we at the federal level can do ourselves. It is something that has to be done in concert with other levels of government, in the community, and with families. There must be a willingness to be more open.
I know the experience that I have had. I am sure other members have had it. I also consider it to be a sad commentary. A co-worker of mine some years ago, a good friend, was totally opposed to abortion. We had many discussions about this. He was absolutely adamant in his views.
I remember some time later that he found out that his 18-year old daughter had gone to the United States one weekend and had an abortion. She felt that she could not go to her father, knowing his views, that it would not be accepted and that she had to go off on her own to do this. He was stricken. I was saddened.
Government Orders
Despite one's personal views about these kinds of issues, surely we have to encourage a more open dialogue among men and women and between parents and children so that we can deal with these issues more effectively and help our young people in ways in which I think they want to be helped. They want that kind of understanding. They need that knowledge, and they need that acceptance.
My plea to my colleagues in the House of Commons today is: yes, support the bill. We need to get on with this and get it behind us. Also, let us work together to ensure that Canadian women truly have options and that we indeed have a greater esteem and respect for Canadian children.

I enjoyed listening to the hon. member. She has given the topic a great deal of thought, time and research, as has almost eveiy speaker who has risen in this House. It takes a topic like this to bring out the true parliamentarian in all of us. I congratulate the speaker for her words.
I was pleased she highlighted that as a Canadian society we treasure life, we protect life. She is right on there. I think that is what makes the Canadian society a little unique, maybe more unique than many other countries. It gives us that identity because we do have this respect for life, this respect for others.
This is why I am having difficulty in trying to analyse why she would support the bill. The hon. member from Trinity-Spadina gave us statistics that for 1987, 63,662 abortions were performed. He was impressed that this was 3,000 less than the year before, but it is still snuffing out the lives of over 63,000 children. This bill will not reduce that. If this bill goes through we will continue to have more than 60,000 to 70,000 lives snuffed out, which goes against Canadian society that treasures life. The minister also said that when someone gets killed in an auto accident we have laws so that one person cannot take the life of another person.
I am one of those who believes that life does begin at conception. I am wondering if the hon. member could clarify how she came to that conclusion, knowing that this bill will snuff out over 60,000 lives a year, and how she can still support the bill.
Just for interest, she also mentioned the right of women to make choices. I called one of the pages and asked for the Oxford Dictionary. I looked up the definition of choices and it said: "variety to choose from". I think that is the beauty of our society too that men and

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
women who are of an age where they want to have sexual encounters have this variety to choose from. If they make the right choice, there will not be life and there will not be a need for abortion.
With her experience in the television program where she was doing the interviewing, I am wondering if she could share with this House how we can teach our young people-and she specifically mentioned the ages 15 to 19-to make the right choices but to make the choices before the pregnancy, before conception, again not requiring so many abortions.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The member has put a number of questions. I am not sure I will have an opportunity to address them all in the question and comment period today.
It comes back to the balance that I see. Yes, we treasure life, but we also treasure the rights of women to make decisions about that. In my mind the woman should be able to make that choice. I hope she makes an informed choice if she is in the situation of having to make it and understands the implication of that choice. She should have the opportunity, as broad an opportunity as possible within the regime that we are putting forward, to make those choices. That just comes from my own view of the world and the way it should be. I would not place the responsibility or the onus on this law or this bill for causing or not causing abortions in itself. There are a variety of reasons that women seek abortions. In my mind at least it is not fair to say that this bill will result in increased abortions. I hope indeed that if we progress as a society we will see fewer abortions.
What do I say to young people? I have three teenagers myself. My daughter and I talk about this quite a lot, actually. She has some very strong views and is quite abhorred by some of the laws she is familiar with in the States where in some cases a young woman would have no access to abortion or a court, a judge has to make that decision. She thinks that is totally wrong and that it should be a decision between a woman and her doctor.
I have tried to instil a sense of responsibility and that there are consequences to actions. You cannot tell young people not to engage in sexual activity. They are going to have to make up their own minds about that. It has changed from my day and young people perhaps act
quite differently now, but I think they have to be prepared for the consequences and therefore take measures, preventive measures. The onus should not only be on the woman. That is one of the things that has always annoyed me in the past, that society has said it is the woman who should take the preventive measures. I think men, young men particularly in this case, have to accept that responsibility as well.
As I said before in my comments this takes education. It takes openness and willingness to talk about it. It is not the approach where you pretend it does not happen. It does happen. It is there. The facts tell us that young people engage in sexual activity. We may have our own views about that, but all we can do is help them through that process and try to assist them in understanding what their responsibilities to themselves and to their own future are as well.
A young girl of 14 or 15 just does not usually have the capacity to look after a young child. Therefore, it is not fair that she should engage in activity that could result in a child being bom, without taking appropriate measures. There should be a lot more willingness to be open on these issues.

It should be clear to the minister how disappointed I personally am, and I imagine many of her constituents are, with this Byzantine rationalization to support this bill.
There are a number of points I want to make. I listened with care to her remarks, and I think those remarks were based on the assumption that the great Canadian compromise will bring some resolution to this very painful debate that we are now engaged in. I would like to ask her to respond to that because I think she and I both know that this is not going to be resolved. This is going to be an ongoing, continuing debate as our society develops.
The other comment I would like to make is that she said: "some bounds are necessary". I would like her to answer whether or not she does not believe that women really are capable of imposing their own bounds on that kind of decision. I think that does speak to the kind of respect the minister has for women and their capacity for making painful decisions.
November 22, 1989

I also would like her to try to get me to understand why she characterizes this bill as fair and workable and why there should be a national standard, because it does not improve any ability for access in this bill.
Finally, I would like her to clarify also her allusion to the Supreme Court decision regarding the foetus in light of the Daigle decision last week which I think made quite clear that the foetus really has no rights unless the child is bom alive.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my understanding of the decision last week by the Supreme Court is that it referred specifically to the Quebec charter, that they have not yet dealt with the other cases before them, so I do not know what their ruling will be.
With respect to access, this bill does not in itself provide or ensure access. We know the difficulties in certain parts of the country. I also recognize that that is a provincial responsibility. Our responsibility at the federal level is providing the legal framework, and a legal framework which I believe will be more conducive because it will be a national standard. Ultimately, if a province is not providing the service and it is taken to court, it would provide greater justification to be able to be successful in such a case.
I believe compromise is essential in a democracy. I know we all have very strong views about different issues and that this is the place we express and debate those views. We will never really be able to get on with things unless we are prepared to compromise.
I have talked to people from newly developing democracies, to Mrs. Aquino who was here recently, about the difficulties they are having in the new Philippine Parliament, as well as to others in other Parliaments.
One of the difficulties is that people have not been used to this aspect, that you have to be prepared to compromise. If you just hold stringently to two opposing grounds you will never get anywhere. We do that within our caucus and I am sure within the caucus of the hon. member. This is the only way you can move forward. You have to come to a compromise so that you can move ahead with a position which you believe is probably in the best interests of the whole, although it might not be what you prefer personally.
Government Orders
In this case, yes, it is a compromise. We have all admitted that. We have all had to put some water in our wine, as the Prime Minister said, but I believe in the interests of not resolving the issue forever. I know it will not be. I know it will continue to be debated. However, for the majority of Canadians-and this is certainly the feedback that I have had in my riding-this is an appropriate compromise in balancing the different points of view and different interests involved in this issue. Perhaps it is a typical but an appropriate Canadian compromise.

Madam Speaker, it is my honour today and in fact my duty, as it is the duty of every member of this House, to address these very important issues. We have now come to a point where decisions should be made. The decisions that are before us are: When do we terminate a pregnancy, what rights do individuals have in our society, and what are the rights of the unborn child from the moment of conception?
This government has brought in legislation, Bill C-43, which it hopes will address these problems. I suggest that the legislation does not address the problems. The legislation in no way goes anywhere near correcting the problems before the House. Therefore, the legislation is
fundamentally flawed. It should be turned down and sent back to this government for reconsideration and redrafting. Then a new piece of legislation could come before this House. It is the duty of the House to bring forth acceptable legislation, and this legislation is certainly not acceptable in its present form.
Let me deal first with some of the arguments that we have heard and have been hearing since the introduction of Bill C-43 from both sides. We hear that at least we now have some legislation, inadequate as it is, but it is better to have this legislation than no legislation at all, inasmuch as no legislation at all allows abortion on demand.
The other thing we hear is: let's get this bill into committee, then at committee stage we can make some amendments and bring it back before this House with the amendments we want.
We also hear that we should draft the amendments, approve them, incorporate them into the legislation, bring the bill before this House, pass it, but before it receives Royal Assent, send it to the Supreme Court of Canada on a reference to test its authenticity, to see if it would pass Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I say that these arguments do not hold water. They are not acceptable. It is the duty of the governing party to bring forth legislation, and it is the duty of the opposition to challenge, correct and refine legislation before the House. In this instance it is the duty, then, of each of us in our own conscience to reject or accept the proposed law. It is still the fundamental duty of this government to legislate, but what it has done in this instance is bring forth a very neutral proposal. The legislation before us lacks in total substance. In fact it has very little substance at all.
When the Minister of Justice proposed this legislation, he said in this House on November 7 that the new abortion law had as its overriding objective the balancing of interests-the rights and interests of women, society's interest, and the protection of the foetus. This legislation does not realize these objectives. It does not satisfy those who oppose the termination of pregnancy, and it certainly does not satisfy those who prefer choice as to whether that pregnancy should be terminated.
November 22, 1989

The law that was struck down on January 28, 1988, in the Morgentaler case, and then the law that was stated by the Supreme Court on November 16, 1989, said that no one has the right to seek an injunction depriving a woman of her right to terminate the pregnancy.
The proposed legislation that we have before us is contrary to this decision. It invites any third party to press criminal charges against a woman or a doctor if there is evidence of an unlawful early termination of pregnancy.
Bill C-43 may be in violation of the Charter of Rights since it in effect removes all choice from the woman, leaving the decision entirely in the hands of a physician. We as legislators, I suggest, cannot abrogate our rights to the courts or to the medical profession. It is the duty of the courts to interpret legislation; it is a duty of the medical profession to heal; and it is the duty of this House to form legislation.
The government has said in this legislation that the decision for the early termination of pregnancies should be left entirely in the hands of the physician. We hear of the Morgentaler decision; we hear of the Morgentaler clinics. We hear the name of Morgentaler but we never hear of the preface. It is not Mr. Morgentaler or Master Morgentaler, it is Dr. Morgentaler. I ask, is this the type of person who will be making decisions on whether or not pregnancies should be terminated?
The bill is pro choice for doctors but has no choice for women. I think it removes all discretionary rights from the woman in her visits to the doctor. The Chief Justice said on January 28, when he struck down the present law, that to carry a foetus to term, unless she meets certain criteria related to her own priorities and aspirations, is profound interference with the woman's body, and this is a violation of the person. I suggest that the proposed legislation before this House is open to challenge on the same grounds as the former law.
Let me discuss one of the fundamental issues that this legislation lacks and that is the rights of the unborn child. This legislation certainly does not address this issue. Joseph Borowski failed to assert fetal rights because there was no longer an abortion law upon which
Government Orders
to base a challenge. The proposed legislation does not address the rights of the unborn.
As we discuss the rights of the unborn, just for a few moments let us remove any thoughts of religion from the equation, because this is the area where we run into some difficulty from a religious aspect or from our own beliefs. The greatest thing left to us, with the removal of God or religion from the argument, is life itself.
Even the most radical secular person, the most hedonistic of individuals, must struggle at some time with the fundamental question of when life begins, when life ends, under what circumstances life can be ended, when life must be protected, and what authority in our society protects life? Is it our legal authorities, medical authorities or our church authorities who protect life in our society, or is it a combination of these elements?
In our society, what protection do we extend to the lives of the helpless, the dying, the aged, and the unborn? We must look at all of these phases of life.
Even if some scientists or theologians state that in the early stages of pregnancy we cannot discern human life, the fact remains that the potential of human life is indisputably there. I believe there should be some respect and some caution if the potential is there. At the veiy least, the potential for life exists and that should unequivocally be respected.
As I was putting together some thoughts about this submission I received in the mail this morning a letter from a Mr. and Mrs. Kowalski. They said something that I want to include in my remarks:
Visit your aged mother or grandmother and kiss them tenderly; give your spouse, or your friend a warm hug; take a child's hand, or let an infant grasp your finger and look in their eyes, all the time remembering that the only difference between the very oldest and the very youngest is only "time". Their humanity has not changed!
I suggest that the legislation before us today is about life but it fails and fails badly in dealing with life. Let me close by saying that I am glad that I had the opportunity to address this issue. It is so important that I am able to close on the aspect of when life begins and I thank you for the opportunity of being able to address this issue.

If there are some restrictions on the meaning of "health", the restrictions are likely to be vague enough to invite wide-scale abuse. Those, and similar terms, have no legal or medical definition, and are therefore subject to the most liberal interpretation.
The abortion mentality attacks the absolute value of human life and seeks to replace it with a relative value which allows human life to be destroyed if it is unwanted, inconvenient, an economic burden or handicapped. Either by our own action or our own apathy, we are determining the kind of society we will leave to our children. We must ask ourselves: Will it be a caring society, nurturing the helpless and protecting the vulnerable, or will it be a cruel society discarding the socially and economically inconvenient and disguising its cruelty as concern for the quality of life?
We often hear from the pro-choice forces about a woman's freedom to choose. We all value our right to free choice regarding our vocation, our religion, and our goals in life. Another slogan of the pro-abortion group is: Should not every child be a wanted child? This slogan makes the faulty assumption that unless the child is wanted, he or she is of no value and can be eliminated by abortion. A child cannot be considered merely as property to be disposed of at will. Today, in Canada, there are so many couples waiting to adopt that it has come to the point that many agencies refuse to take new applicants. Yet some 65,000 children are aborted each year because they are unwanted.

Since we have had virtually abortion on demand in Canada since 1969 and have done away with an estimated 1,200,000 children, the problem of child abuse has not been eliminated but rather has increased to epidemic proportions.

The question has been raised that should we not care about the woman's problem? Undoubtedly we must, but our concern should not mean contempt for the life of the unborn child. Since 1969, over 2,000 crisis pregnancy centres have been established across North America by pro-life volunteers and others, to give practical assistance to both mother and child during pregnancy and post-partum adjustment.
Abortions performed because of serious maternal health problems, rape, incest or foetal abnormality, account for no more than 2 per cent of all abortions performed in Canada. A full 98 per cent of abortions occur for social or economic convenience.

Mr. Speaker, today I rise to address an issue that has a long and sordid past in the history of our nation. The abortion issue evokes the greatest emotion in people at the very mention of the word. I have seen for some time now that all people, young and old, have an opinion on this issue, whether it stems from the religious, socio-economic or educational backgrounds or from personal experience.
My opinion stems from a fundamental respect for the sanctity of human life, human life which I believe begins at conception. This is not only what I believe. It is a belief that is held by the majority of the constituents in my riding of Hillsborough, constituents who have written to me over the past year and with whom I have spoken many times. These people have expressed a great concern with the developments that have occurred in the abortion arena over the past year and a half.
Since January, 1988, we have seen a virtual saga of events unfold as a consequence of the Supreme Court's ruling in the Morgentaler case. The Supreme Court ruled that the old abortion law did not comply with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. A year later we saw Mr. Borowski's attempt to have foetal rights defined denied by the Supreme Court of Canada since the Morgentaler decision left the nation without an abortion law upon which they could base a decision.
This was, as many people said, an open invitation to Parliament to deal with this issue. The government, however, did not respond despite calls for a new law from around the country. The Daigle and Dodd cases which we witnessed this past summer demonstrated just how serious an issue this has become. Cases such as this also help to shape our opinion as a nation on this fundamental, social and ethical question.
It is through the unravelling of such events that the federal government has been given an opportunity to introduce abortion legislation so that we can break free from the chaotic state of lawlessness which extends from coast to coast. This situation disturbs millions of Canadians who have written to their members of Parliament asking that Parliament enact legislation to protect the rights of the foetus from the moment of conception. The
government has ignored the feeling that seems to prevail across the country.
The legislation at hand fails to define the rights of the foetus, thus the unacceptable nature of this legislation.
In July, 1988, members of this House were given the opportunity to participate in a multiple choice vote so that government could sense the mood of the House. It was thought that the results of such votes would be taken into consideration when abortion legislation was drafted. Of the five motions voted on at that time, the one that received the most votes was the most pro life and did not call for abortion on demand. The government chose not to introduce legislation to this effect and, instead, allowed the state of lawlessness resulting from the Morgentaler decision to prevail.
The next stumbling block proved to be Mr. Borowski's case. The government did not want to introduce legislation until the Supreme Court made its ruling on this issue of foetal rights. The climax of the ensuing state of lawlessness came with the Daigle and Dodd court cases of the past summer. The anticlimactic end of this saga came on November 3 when the government finally tabled its long-awaited legislation, legislation that I feel does not adequately address the problem at hand.
We have been presented with legislation which is, in effect, a compromise between two opposing forces, legislation which virtually changes nothing and pleases no one. The difference between this bill and the old law is simple. The federal government is now advocating abortion on demand; subject, of course, to the arbitrary decision of a medical doctor regarding its effect on a woman's mental, physical or psychological health. Gone are the days when a therapeutic abortion committee could objectively interpret a need for an abortion.
Abortion is a crime, an act that injures another human being at its most vulnerable stage in development. It is the intentional destruction of a human life, life that begins at the moment of conception with the fusion of the ovum and the sperm. At this time, the first cell of a distinct human being is formed and the colour of the child's eyes and the child's hair is determined. Cell division takes place within hours after conception. A heart beat is present at 25 days and the cerebral cortex at 33 days. Forty-five days after conception, the child's body is complete. At this point, the pregnant woman is

carrying a distinct human being, with arms, legs, fingers and toes which are visible by ultrasound.
Two months after conception, organs and body systems are in place. At this point, many women may not even be aware of the miracle which is taking place. At 12 weeks the movement of muscles and nerves are synchronized so that the arms and legs can move and the child is also sensitive to touch, heat, sound and pain.
It is difficult to believe that it takes only 12 weeks for a human foetus to reach such a level of development. At this time all of the body functions and parts that children will develop as they grow are present. When we learn that human development has such distinct stages, it is alarming to hear that 87.8 per cent of all abortions performed in 1986 were completed before the thirteenth week of pregnancy. The common belief is that a foetus is not viable until it reaches 20 weeks, but when its development is broken down in such a manner, one sees that this is not the case.
Such information is used in order to appease the sentiments of those who justify the act of performing an abortion before the foetus is viable. The survival of the foetus is threatened if full development is not reached. Abortion is an act that affects not only the life of the mother, but the life that the mother has created in union with the child's father.
What, may I ask, could be more tragic than to allow a human being with the capability of feeling pain and hearing the human voice and that has all of the body parts intrinsic to life outside of the womb to be terminated at will by abortion.
All abortions must be criminalized. Our criminal law is a reflection of who we are as a society. It defines the interests of our society that are worthy of protection and respect against those that are not. Laws which dictate such policy mirror our societal beliefs and values. I believe as Canadians we must demonstrate a fundamental respect for human life. As a result, I believe all abortions should be banned in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to address a very sensitive and difficult issue which has moral, ethical, religious, and often very personal meanings for every Canadian. I am referring, of course, to the issue of abortion.
The new legislation recognizes that abortion is a medical decision to be arrived at by a woman and her medical practitioner based on health grounds. Three principles guide the new legislation: one, balancing the woman's constitutional rights with society's interest in the foetus; two, ensuring that fair and reasonable access to abortion is not denied; three, ensuring that all abortions are performed by qualified medical practitioners based on health grounds.
The bill before the House is reasonable. It provides for the legal entitlement to abortion by the following means: the bill proposes to eliminate administrative impediments found in the old law and struck down in Morgental-er and a woman seeking an abortion is required to secure the opinion of a single medical practitioner stating that the continuation of pregnancy would likely be a threat to life or to health. General health grounds for permitting an abortion have been identified by the medical profession and by the courts as including mental, physical and psychological health.
The bill also requires that a medical practitioner's assessment as to the threats to life or health be rooted in generally accepted standards of the medical profession, and the new bill provides definitions as to the meaning of "health", "medical practitioner", "medical opinion" and "inducing abortion".
The proposed legislation comes under the Criminal Code because it is only through the power of the criminal law that Parliament can legislate entitlement to abortion on a national basis. I truly deplore the fact that the legislative measures that we are proposing involve the Criminal Code. But, as we have said on many occasions in this House, this is the only way to proceed at the national level if we want to enable Canadian women, in any province all across the country, to have the right to the services of this medical procedure.
I firmly believe Parliament should legislate with respect to abortion and that is why I am speaking today. I do firmly believe that the decision to have an abortion is a medical decision that rests with the woman, her physician, and her God; her beliefs, her morals, her standards. And yes, all abortions should be and must be performed by a licensed physician for it is a recognized medical procedure.
I support the Canadian Medical Association which is opposed to abortion being legislated under the Criminal Code or other federal laws. The physician will have the responsibility of making the medical decision on whether a continuation of the pregnancy would, or is likely to, threaten the life or the physical, mental or psychological health of the patient. The physician will have to make a decision on an individual basis according to accepted standards of medical practice. Could the physician be charged? Practically never, except, of course, under extreme circumstances. And the Supreme Court judgment made public last week to all intents and purposes
November 22, 1989

rules out third-party intervention. The unanimous ruling removed the legal basis for obtaining court injunctions to block abortions anywhere in Canada.
For most women the decision to have an abortion is one of the most difficult decisions they will ever have to make. It has implications for the woman, for the family and for all people, because most of us really hold deeply religious views. The decision requires careful thought and analysis.
Counselling is extremely important and I believe all women deserve to be informed, to be informed about the effects of an abortion and, more important, to be informed of all the means available to carry the pregnancy to term. However, once a woman decides to have the medical procedure, the abortion, it is her decision. Family life education is really truly necessary in the school curriculum right across the country. Young people must be taught about the values of life, of love, of sexual relations, responsibility, and understanding. I recognize that family life education is under provincial jurisdiction but surely today we can pledge time to teach our children and all people the responsibility of the human body, the responsibility of pregnancy, the responsibility of life.
Legislation is absolutely necessary and Canadians are demanding it. We can all do without the shocking display, the horror we all witnessed last summer and, of course, I am referring to the Daigle-Tremblay and the Dodd cases.
In a perfect world abortion would not be necessary. We all know, however, that the world is not perfect and that abortions are sometimes necessary. For this reason we must face the issue of abortion as best we can as individuals, as Members of Parliament and as a government. We must try to come up with a reasonable solution to this very sensitive and difficult issue.
I do not claim that Bill C-43 is perfect. I do want to say that we must rise above that which might divide us and seek common ground that is acceptable to the majority. Our most dependable guideposts are tolerance, understanding and maturity. I believe women, in consultation with their physicians, have the right to an abortion. It is

I would like to take this time to point out some of the flaws in the legislation. This new bill places the responsibility squarely on the shoulders of the doctor whose final decision will be based on the generally accepted standards of the medical profession. However, there is no guarantee that all physicians in Canada would apply the same standards and criteria in assessing the health of a pregnant woman.
What if a doctor runs his practice like a business? Also there is no guarantee that a physician's moral and religious values will not influence his assessment of the need for an abortion. In my view, this places a very heavy burden on the medical profession. First, the doctor has the ultimate responsibility of the decision. Second, there is nothing to prevent the father of the child from challenging the doctor's decision and ultimately pressing charges of malpractice.
The bill does not address the issue of foetal rights. The government has chosen to exclude a time restriction which would ban abortion after a certain period in the pregnancy. I am deeply concerned with Madam Justice Wilson's comment concerning the permissible timing of abortion. She said: "The precise point in the development of the foetus, at which the state's interest in its protection becomes compelling, I leave to the informed judgment of the legislature, which is in a position to receive guidance on the subject from all the relevant disciplines. It seems to me, however, that it might fall somewhere in the second trimester".
In my view this statement is irresponsible and inhuman. At six months, premature babies are able to survive due to modern medical technology. I would never agree to an amendment which allows an abortion at such a late stage. It would be a most brutal attack on the weakest of human beings, the foetus, which is at the mercy of circumstances.
It is also unfortunate that the bill was not accompanied by counselling, programs addressing these issues would have provided alternatives to those who seek abortion as the solution for an unplanned pregnancy. To quote the Minister of Health: "There are 150,000 young, single, low-income parents in need of assistance. If we take away the economic reasons for abortion, we would ensure that children are brought into the world and properly cared for".
This statement is further supported by the Council of Bishops of Canada and I quote its president: "Moreover, we reaffirm that a new abortion law must be developed in the context of other policies and programs which address the social and economic conditions which contribute to abortion". What is being said is, let us not put a patch on the problem, let us try and minimize this last resort. I must reiterate again, let us have programs that will provide the people of this country with some alternatives.
I can only hope that a Conservative government will see its way clear on this matter and will institute programs which will give the woman an option and therefore give the right to life to the unborn child and the opportunity to reach his or her full potential. There is absolutely no reason in a country as rich as ours that some children are denied.

Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings that I rise in the House today to speak on the abortion legislation. I hope that everyone would agree with me when I state that there should never be a need for an abortion, that an abortion should never take place, because ideally, an abortion should never be required. Unfortunately, that is not the reality of the situation. We must accept the fact that we do not live in a perfect world. Regardless of our position on this most personal issue, we must resolve this situation to the best of our abilities within the framework society has laid down.
I believe there are two fundamental realities that must be addressed before we review the legislation itself at this stage of debate.
First, a bill must pass the test of Parliament. It must be designed and worded in such a way as to reflect and gain the support of the majority of parliamentarians. Without such consensus any law cannot be enacted or implemented. Second, a bill must be able to stand the test of the Charter of Rights. It must reflect the views of society without infringing on the rights and freedoms of individuals as outlined in the Charter. It must be deemed constitutional and therefore stand up under a challenge to the Supreme Court of Canada.
This government has shown strong leadership in drafting a bill that encompasses these democratic requirements. Although for many of us on both sides of this issue the legislation does not reflect our personal convictions, it is still a valid piece of legislation that warrants our discussion and our thoughts. As legislators and also
November 22, 1989

residents of this democratic society our personal views must often be tempered by the restraints inherent in this institution.
Yes, we can all take individual stands based on our sentiment and emotion and personal beliefs, but without consensus we will not accomplish anything except going back to square one without any valid legislation. Or we can reach a majority agreement, through compromise, that reflects both our individual beliefs and yet supports the legislation that best demonstrates the consensus in this country.
Concessions, no matter how unpalatable, may be necessary from all parties if effective leadership and direction is to be shown by the members of this Elouse to the country. Any law dealing with abortion must protect the sanctity of life. It must recognize not only the rights of the living, but also of the unborn. In other words, in dealing with and recognizing the rights of the woman we must also acknowledge society's responsibility to protect those who cannot protect themselves.
The Supreme Court of Canada, in its decision on December 28, 1988, indicated that any federal policy or law on abortion should not deny Canadian women fair and reasonable access to abortion, should protect the constitutional rights of women to security of the person, should reflect, as a valid federal objective, the state's interest in the foetus and should protect the health of the woman at all stages.
As a result, this new legislation attempts to balance women's constitutional rights and society's interest in protecting the foetus, it ensures that fair and reasonable access to abortion is not denied and it ensures that any abortions are performed by qualified medical practitioners based on the physical, mental or psychological health of the woman.
A woman seeking an abortion under this legislation is now required to seek the opinion of her medical practitioner. The physician's decision to proceed with an abortion based on generally accepted standards of the medical profession must show that the continuation of the pregnancy would likely threaten her health or her life.
This recognizes that life begins at conception. I believe this legislation reflects society's interest in protecting the foetus, and yet at the same time it also recognizes the rights of women to maintain positive health. The term
Government Orders
"positive health", as defined by the World Health Organization and adopted by our Ministry of National Health and Welfare, means: "a state of complete, physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity". This also clearly reinforces the woman's constitutional rights to security of the person.
The woman, like the medical practitioner, must follow the legal requirements as stipulated in Bill C-43 which balances her rights with those of the foetus. Therefore, any woman performing a self-induced abortion or who obtains one outside of the medical profession will be committing an illegal act punishable by prosecution under the Criminal Code.
The potential threats facing doctors under the proposed law in my opinion have been greatly exaggerated. The police will not lay charges without valid evidence, and Crown officials will withdraw charges if they are frivolous. It is entirely possible however that, yes, some will try to abuse the law. But we must have faith that the vast majority of doctors in this country will respect the intention of this law. The inclusion of the abortion provisions into the criminal Code is welcome because as was said by law reform commissioner Joseph Maingot:
The criminal law is our nation's fundamental statement of public policy-Ultimately, the criminal law is a mirror of what we are; it reflects our commitment, or lack of commitment, to human dignity and equality.
There are a number of critics who believe an abortion law is not necessary. I, however, disagree. The situation we found ourselves in last summer and the associated publicity as a result of the Supreme Court decision refutes that argument. A situation was created where the Supreme Court was forced to work in a vacuum, attempting to make a decision based strictly on its legal perspective and not that of society. It is our job as legislators to draft and implement legislation that is based on society's perspective.
There are those who have suggested that education and information regarding proper methods of birth control and research at the scientific level should be improved. This is something that I feel should and could be endorsed by the federal government through the Canada Health Act and would go a long way to assist society as a whole. This is an area that should be explored at the committee or report stage and could form part of the regulations and then be administered

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
through the Health Services and Promotion Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Once the legislation becomes law, if the Supreme Court of Canada cannot resolve cases before it to the satisfaction of the government, then perhaps at that time further amendments, if required, could be introduced to rectify the problems that it encounters.
However, I sincerely feel that the legislation is clear and concise enough for the courts to make clear judgments without any hesitation and without prejudice.
I personally do not believe the present legislation is strong enough to satisfy my pro-life views. However, the present legal void that we find ourselves in is totally unacceptable. We must reach a consensus before more lives are lost.
I am also terrified of the prospect of returning to the bad old days. We must not turn back the clock to a time when women's lives were threatened because they could not obtain a legal abortion. This once prevalent occurrence should be avoided at all costs.
I would support an amendment to this bill to protect the life of the unborn except where the continuation of a pregnancy would or would be likely to endanger the life of the female person. The rationale of such an amendment is that the unborn constitutes human life and that the only possible ground for ending this life is self defence.
