Therefore it is my opinion that the present act will require amending in order to afford full legal protection to this life. I personally would have liked the legislation to be more restrictive. The term "health" could have been more narrowly defined.
I anticipate the opportunity to speak in support of this type of restrictive amendment to Bill C-43 at third reading. Therefore, given the democratic rules of this House, and by that I mean that amendments cannot be made until after second reading, I do at this time support the legislation even though it does not reflect my personal convictions because I know in due course I will be given the opportunity to persuasively present amendments.

I would like to take this opportunity to express my views on this very important matter.

I would first of all like to thank the hundreds of people in my riding of Ottawa Centre and throughout the country who gave me their opinion on this issue. Their letters and calls show deep convictions about the right to life and their feeling that the government must protect it. I am pleased that we can finally debate this complex and difficult issue and grant the wish of Canadians who have asked us to find a solution and bring forward legislation to fill the legal vacuum in which we now find ourselves.
I know, Madam Speaker, that the bill before this House was only tabled after long hours of hard work and painfully personal decisions. Although I am aware of the effort required to draft it, I am afraid that it ignores some basic problems raised in the abortion debate.

I had hoped the new abortion legislation would take a broader look at the social and economic factors that play such a large role in the abortion dilemma. Last year, for example, 65,000 women in Canada made the difficult decision to proceed with abortions. Why does a woman decide to have an abortion? The answers to that question are varied and complex, but I think it is fair to say that many abortions that take place in Canada every year might not have happened if the proper education and support systems had been in place.
Canada is a country renowned for its compassion. Our peace keeping efforts and our diplomatic initiatives have saved countless lives around the world. Our social programs have come to the aid of the disadvantaged and underprivileged within our borders. We must ensure this compassion reaches out equally to the unborn and his mother. We must take this compassion and the intense energy that has been focused on the abortion debate and develop a productive, preventive plan of action.
As a government we must take the challenge to prevent the attitude and situations that are now resulting in abortions. There is no doubt that unplanned and

November 22, 1989

Government Orders
unwanted pregnancies have been found to be an exceedingly difficult dilemma for a pregnant woman.
It may be the most devastating event in her life. What is happening is that many women take this step because they feel that they have no alternative-they are desperate and they have nowhere to go. It is our job as a society and as a government to provide that alternative. We must work to change the attitudes and situations which lead to abortion. It is the government's responsibility to ensure that our citizens have the income, the child care and the emotional support to effectively care for a child.
Educational institutions and health care agencies must share the family doctor's responsibility for providing advice and information on family planning. We need to look at the extent of funding and support being given to family planning services.
Are Canadian women being given all the facts? Are adequate services and support networks in place? If they are, are they accessible?
Counselling and family support services must be readily available and accessible to all Canadians in all walks of life. Each one of us in this House, as well as Canadians across the country, have different views on issues such as abortion and capital punishment. It is my belief that there is not a consensus on this issue, and that there will be no consensus.
Canadians, if they are given the opportunity to vote on this issue, would vote on the basis of their convictions, their beliefs, their upbringing, their education, and the values they hold. I know that in my riding, as well as across Canada, there are those who support the legislation and those who are opposed to it.
For me, while I understand there is no consensus on this issue, it is my responsibility to vote on this matter according to my conscience. During the last election and ever since I have stated publicly that I would be in support of legislation that protects the right of the unborn. Since this legislation does not seem to fulfil this commitment, I find myself compelled to vote against it.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to address the House today on this most important issue. It is an issue which is of concern to all Canadians, but most specifically it concerns Canadian women.
Abortion is being perceived as an issue which divides Canadians. It should not be. We must as a nation show respect for individual decision-making in matters of fundamental personal importance. We must also seek to balance the vital interests of both the mother and the child by permitting an abortion only when the life or the physical, mental or psychological health of the mother is threatened.
As women struggle to develop their place in this modem and constantly evolving society, they are struggling to eliminate discrimination and to develop a set of legislative reforms which ensures this. Women's needs are being translated into protected rights. The right to reproduce or not to reproduce is a right which women recognize as fundamental to their dignity. Therefore, when formulating our legislation, we must listen to what women are saying and we must formulate legislation which will best serve the universal requirements of Canadian women.
The decision to proceed with an abortion is probably one of the most difficult any woman will be called upon to make. It is a decision which will have lasting ramifications on her life. The factors determining the decision are the result of previous life experiences, personal conscience and personal moral values. No two women will experience life in the same way. That is why a woman must enjoy the democratic rights afforded her in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which allow her to arrive at her own decision.
Legislation in this issue of abortion is necessary to prevent further highly publicized and, for the participants, emotionally draining judicial confrontations. In a recent decision members of the Supreme Court unanimously stated:
There is no foetal right to life contained in the vague wording of
Quebec's Charter of Rights nor under the province's Civil code or
the common law that prevails throughout the rest of Canada.
This statement re-emphasizes the fact that matters related to this issue should not be resolved in the courtroom. The courts will uphold the laws that we the legislators put in place. So when proposed legislation is being drafted it is essential to ensure that it reflects the greater public good and that it will withstand legal scrutiny. We must provide for Canadians a law which establishes a uniform national standard.

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
Abortions, when deemed to be necessary, should be accessible in every region and to all female citizens. Location and financial resources should not be factors in such an emotional and a personal decision. I am convinced that Bill C-43 will meet those requirements.
Each year in Canada, about 360,000 children are bom and about 65,000 abortions take place. Over half of these abortions are performed on women under the age of 25.
This debate on abortion, by emphasizing the fact that so many abortions are performed on young women, may produce a positive effect. We know there is an urgent need to better educate our young people on the prevention of unwanted pregnancies. Our goal must be to reduce the number of abortions by concentrating on education and information accessibility. Counselling services, family planning services and information on contraception must be readily available to all Canadians.
The provision of advice and information on family planning and human sexuality falls to the family physician, but that responsibility must also be shared by the educational institutions and health care agencies.
Frank and open discussion on this issue will help to illuminate the dilemma and hopefully will result in positive advancements which will make abortions unnecessary.
The Canadian Medical Association is pleased that the proposed legislation recognizes that abortion is a medical act. It supports the concept of abortion being decided upon within the doctor-patient relationship. It does have concerns related to the issue of abortion which are also shared by many Canadians. The association is concerned that all patients should be provided with the option of full and immediate counselling services in the event of unwanted pregnancies.
Since the risk of complications of induced abortion are lowest in early pregnancy, early diagnosis of pregnancy and determination of appropriate management should be encouraged. There should be no delay in the provision of abortion services.
However, no patient should be compelled to have a pregnancy terminated. No physician should be compelled to participate in the termination of a pregnancy. A physician whose moral or religious beliefs prevent him or
her from recommending or performing an abortion should inform the patient of such so that she may consult another physician. No discrimination should be directed against doctors who do not perform or assist at induced abortions.
Abortion services should meet specific standards in the areas of counselling, informed choice, medical and surgical procedures, nursing and follow-up care.
We should look to the areas of research and development in the health care field for advanced methods of contraception. Our goal should be to reduce that number of 65,000 abortions, not by restricting choice but by encouraging greater choice in contraception.
Organizations such as the Planned Parenthood Federation encourage choices by educating, promoting and supporting family planning. This organization recognizes that each community is different and implements programs sensitive to the varying needs of each one.
All children bom into this world have a right to be anticipated with love. That is the hope, I am sure, of all of us in this Chamber. That is their fundamental right. How can we best ensure that this will be? We must utilize all the avenues that have been offered to us, through the knowledge we have gained over time, through our education and life experience, to bring in the fairest legislation possible for all Canadians.
If and when a woman is called upon to make this crucial decision, we must afford her the benefit of her knowledge, education and experience to make the right decision for herself and her child.
I would like to end my speech this evening by referring to remarks made by Justice Bertha Wilson on this issue upon rendering a decision in the Morgentaler case in 1988.
Liberty in a free and democratic society does not require the state
to approve the personal decisions made by its citizens; it does,
however, require the state to respect them.
In summation, it seems to me that what Canadian women are asking for is the fundamental right to make a choice which is right for them on an issue which is a deeply personal and private matter. Should guidance be sought, it should be readily available to every woman through our health care services.
November 22, 1989

In a free and democratic society, all members of that society have their rights and their responsibilities. I have no doubt that the women of this country are fully capable of accepting their responsibilities as full and equal partners.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the previous speaker for her remarks, which I think women will appreciate.
I rise today to summarize my opposition to Bill C-43 and to suggest steps that this government can take to lessen the need for abortions.
Recently I received a long and thoughtful letter from an Ontario woman who sent her views on abortion to all MPs. In it she said:
There is nothing that you will ever do in life that will affect your life
as much as becoming a parent, and it is irreversible. You can become
unfat; you can become unemployed; you can become unmarried; you
can even become unordinary; but you can never become unparented.
It is not to be taken lightly or forced on anyone.
I strongly believe that women of Canada must have the personal freedom to choose to be a parent. In this way children will be loved and wanted. Hopefully, a woman and her partner will be able to provide the loving care and opportunities that children need to grow to maturity.
However, many women are not in a position to do this and for a variety of reasons may decide to terminate an unwanted pregnancy. This is a very personal and often a very difficult emotional decision.
If a woman decides on an abortion, access to safe medical procedures must be available to terminate a pregnancy as early as possible.
The Supreme Court decision last week on the Daigle case sends a strong message. Judges agreed that a woman has the right to choose whether or not to terminate a pregnancy. There is no basis in law to recognize the foetus as a person.
I will be voting against Bill C-43 because I am strongly opposed to recriminalizing abortion. I do not want the state interfering in a matter that is a very personal and intimate female decision, a reproductive right that should only require consultation between a woman and her doctor.
Government Orders
The medical profession already has health regulations and standards that apply to medical procedure. We do not need criminal sanctions.
Many speakers from my party have explained why we oppose Bill C-43, which is an amendment to the Criminal Code that prohibits abortion at all stages of pregnancy, unless a doctor decides that the continuation of the pregnancy would threaten the woman's physical, psychological or mental health. This bill reduces access to abortion by threatening doctors with criminal penalties of up to two years in prison unless vaguely defined health criteria are met. It ignores the real issue of unwanted pregnancy. We will see more court actions and third party interventions as a result of the bill.
Access is limited. Many healthy woman, and particularly young girls who my colleagues said are 50 per cent of those seeking abortions for a variety of reasons, may not qualify. They will be forced to lie to a doctor or go to a back-street abortionist.
I am sickened at heart by extremists who are so autocratic that they want state interference to curtail a woman from having an abortion. I feel that those who support criminal sanctions are victimizing pregnant women. Like Chantal Daigle's ex-boyfriend, some want to force women to continue unwanted pregnancies unless there is a health problem.
Doctors also are victimized and scapegoated. They are placed in the role of judge and face a jail term, and as a result may interpret health very narrowly.
Undoubtedly, many poor women will not have access to abortions, and healthy adolescents may not qualify.
This law is degrading, judgmental and intrudes on the rights and privacy of women. Why are women not trusted and respected to make their own decisions, if and when they want to have children? Why do women need to be controlled by a patriarchal society? Why is the focus all on women as if men had no responsibility for pregnancies?
It takes two to achieve an unwanted pregnancy and to cause the need for an abortion. If this law were to be applied equally under the Criminal Code, perhaps we should have an amendment that would require the prevention of unwanted pregnancies.

Government Orders
What are the responsibilities of men to their sexual partners? Should vasectomies be required in law unless a pregnancy is planned by both partners and fathers agree to support their progeny? This would be one way to eliminate abortions.
Of course, we do not want this kind of state interference to require sexually active men to be more responsible to sexual partners. However, too many men ignore the fact that birth control and responsible family planning are a man's responsibility, not just the woman's.
Mutual decisions to have a family result in wanted children. This should be society's goal.
This bill discriminates against women because it deals only with women's role in reproduction. In many ways it does not comply with international agreements to which Canada is a signator. For example, the UN Convention on Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women in Article 2(g) requires a "repeal of all the national penal provisions which constitute discrimination against women". We are creating a new provision under Bill C-43.
This convention and the UN Forward Looking Strategies, as well as the UN Population Plan Of Action, all make it clear that family planning must be available to all women. Yet this government continues to contravene these agreements by drastically cutting funds to Planned Parenthood.
If the government wanted to do something about abortion, it could ensure access. It could reinstate the funding for Planned Parenthood that it cut. It could perform research into safe, effective means of contraception. It could put the support services and programs in place that pregnant women and parents need to raise a child.
The only law we need is one to ensure access, not restrict access. This is not a matter for criminal law but for amendments to the Canada Health Act.
Abortion should only be a last resort. Society can do a lot to prevent unwanted pregnancies. Research by Planned Parenthood indicates that the provision of reproductive health services and sex education reduces the rate of teenage pregnancies. Clearly, not enough is being done in this area as research also shows that one in six teenage girls will become pregnant before turning 20.
Although the government self-righteously insists it has raised funding to Planned Parenthood, this is misleading.
Planned Parenthood received $447,000 in 1979, and this was reduced to $139,000 in 1988, a paltry sum for such an essential service. I urge the government to further increase funding for Planned Parenthood and for community groups that provide family education and accessible contraception services.
Sex education in schools should be encouraged. The government should also re-establish a family planning division at Health and Welfare where there is only one full-time staff person.
The federal government must increase funding for research into reliable forms of contraception for men as well as women.
Health problems associated with IUDs and the pill are of great concern to women. Why has the government neglected this research which could prevent abortions in the future?
Although attitudes are changing, and I am very pleased many younger men in our society are sharing the joys and responsibilities of parenting, women still do bear the brunt of child rearing. Whether or not she has a spouse a woman is usually expected to fulfil the demanding task of caring for and raising children as well as working outside the home.
Child maintenance payments continue to be inadequate or nonexistent, and women are left to raise children alone and in poverty. Governments must enforce maintenance payments more effectively and ensure family incomes above the poverty line.
It is a national disgrace that one in five children are poor and that 150,000 kids use food banks each month. After years of studying government promises we still do not have a national child care program. We urgently need -a child care system that is universally accessible, affordable, non-profit, and of high quality. We must also extend parental leave with UI benefits to cover at least 26 weeks. Family policy should be encouraged in the workplace so parents can spend more time with children, with flexible hours and family leave.
In conclusion, I implore all members to spend as much time next year as we have spent this year on this abortion

debate in order to promote policies that will reduce the need for abortion and programs that will support children and provide for their care.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House today and make my contribution to the debate on Bill C-43.
Madam Speaker, all Canadians were appalled last summer when they heard about the Chantal Daigle case on radio, television and through the other media.
I do not think anyone would want to go through an experience that must have been quite terrible, to see one's private life dragged through the newspapers and flaunted on television, especially a life as full of controversy and incidents as that particular one. I think we all agree we would not want to repeat that experience.
However, where we do not agree, and I think here our differences are almost irreconcilable, is on how to solve this problem.
I truly believe that the Bill before the House today does not deal with the problem. It would need a number of amendments before it could do so even partially. I would even go so far as to say that whatever we put into the bill, the problem will never be solved.
In fact, the problem is a social one. I feel that any bill that does not recognize this fact will never provide a solution, and quite frankly, it would be no more than an exercise in camouflage that ignores the real problem.
One paragraph of this Bill shows a tendency to criminalize, where it says that a physician who induces an abortion where there is no threat to the mother's health is liable to a maximum of two years' imprisonment.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think putting people in prison is the ideal solution, because it does not deal with the problem. Women will continue to have abortions, despite the restrictions we put into this bill.
So what do we need to tackle the roots of the problem? We need a family policy, supported by a tax policy. It is a fact that, be it unintentionally, our federal and provincial laws do not support the family and even tend to destroy it. Let me explain. As a married man with five children, financially I would be better off abandoning my family, because in that case, I could deduct alimony payments from my income tax. Personally, of
Government Orders
course, I would never do this just to save a few dollars, but there are people out there who might do just that. So as I indicated in my example, and it applies to many other Canadians as well, our laws definitely encourage marital separation and the destruction of the family unit. And that is a sad comment on our society.
I have raised the subject on many occasions, and I intend to go on doing so until something is done about it. What is taking us so long to provide help for needy mothers? I have already talked about wages for women working in the home. Or it could be for a father working in the home, because some fathers stay home to take care of the children, because the mother has died or for whatever reason.
It seems to me that if we tackle the roots of the problem, it would be a lot easier to find a solution that is more humane for all involved. We would not have to take people before the courts, much less put them in prison, because that will never solve the problem. The fact that today, on the threshold of the 21st century, in a civilized country like Canada, we have no solutions at hand to restrict abortion and the destruction of the foetus and of our people and we have found no other solution but to put the doctor in prison, I think shows we are truly lacking in imagination. We will never be able to solve a social problem of this magnitude.
The fact is that no matter what we put into this Bill, a young girl or young woman in dire financial straits, and God knows there are many cases like that, will get an abortion regardless.
I have already suggested that in some cases abortion would be acceptable but only when absolutely necessary, as in cases of rape or incest or when the mother's health is at risk, and when I say her health I mean physical health, not mental or psychological health which, as you know, is very difficult to determine. Today, a woman could go to a doctor, feeling rather desperate. Her doctor would say: "Okay, in that case, since you feel depressed, whether" this is temporary or whatever, I will do an abortion.
Of course any woman who comes to such a decision will not go out and celebrate. If she comes to such a decision, it is because she is really hurt inside and does not know where to turn. We already know that; the doctor does not have to justify it.

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
So we might as well then have abortion on demand, because it comes to the same thing. But in the case that I just described, I see no need for the woman and her doctor to provide any health reason whatever. If the woman's health is threatened, if her physical health is threatened, if she is pregnant following rape or incest, in that case, I see no need for the woman or doctor to produce a medical document showing that her health is threatened. I was prepared to be more liberal than that in such a case and accept abortion on demand, perhaps with a certain time limit, because the bill before us sets no limit. In that case, it is up to the physician. Even if the foetus is eight months old, he can still perform an abortion. Nothing forbids it.
If we were to consider the problem first and attack it at its roots, we would have to change first of all our policies, our tax legislation, to make it less discriminatory or not discriminatory at all, because God knows it is discriminatory. Let us support families, single mothers, even married women, because they can sometimes be in equally difficult situations.
If we did that, Mr. Speaker, I assure you that the abortion problem would be reduced, if not completely, at least to a very large extent. That would be much more effective, instead of providing punitive measures such as sending the doctor or mother or anyone else to prison- that will not solve the problem. In a way, we are acting unconsciously, and for this reason, I ask my colleagues to think a little. I have already pointed out several times here some injustices that affect young people, especially in Quebec, where those who are under 30 get only one third as much welfare as those who are 30 or over. This situation creates juvenile delinquents and repeat offenders whom I would consider victims rather than criminals. We must ask ourselves the question, Mr. Speaker. Since my time is up, I thank you for listening to me.

Mr. Speaker, there is no need for me to remind the House of the deep anguish and soul searching the issue of abortion has created in the Canadian community. As we explore new ways to generate human life, the sincere fears and questions of community groups and individuals grow in intensity. At the same time, we are a nation proud of its steady movement toward a more equal partnership of men and
women and a fuller commitment to the individual rights of all citizens.
For myself, I would like to go on record at this time as a citizen against abortion and seriously concerned for the protection of the human foetus. However, in spite of that deep personal belief, I am committed to serving all of my constituents as their elected representative. I must find, therefore, a more balanced position for my community as a whole.
Few of us could cast a vote for or against abortion and claim that our vote represents a clear majority of our citizens. In this case, it seems to me that to stand in Parliament absolutely for individual rights or absolutely for foetal protection is an heroic act that is all too easy. It fails to provide leadership to our troubled and divided communities.
If ours were an ideal community in which every child bom was guaranteed the love, nurture and social support essential to happiness, if I were confident that every child bom would be valued and protected by our social system, then I could stand here today confidently and say no to any abortion. But, it seems to me, the steady erosion of universal social support by the current government casts a deep shadow on the hopes for such a social climate. So I have no alternative but to search for balance.
The internationally renowned Canadian scholar, Northrop Frye, has written a great deal on the nature of our culture and our unique qualities as a nation. One very distinct image and attitude he describes is our obsession with the two-sided legend. He says we are always conscious of the double ledger and the need to find balance between conflicting values. While we have sometimes been ridiculed for this as being too low key, too middle of the road, we have built our credibility throughout the world on this willing sense of balance. Our successful history is one of compromise. We seek laws, institutions and expectations in which contrary yet mutually essential human needs and values are sustained in some acceptable and even pragmatic manner.
When history and generations of the future call us to account for our actions in this momentous social issue, we will not be judged by our heroic extremes but by our sensible balance of voices and value systems. If there was ever a need for this Canadian consciousness, this awareness of the double ledger, it is in regard to the difficult and cmcial issue of abortion. At moments it may seem to we politicians more a double-edged sword than an opportunity for balance. Yet, I do believe that this
November 22, 1989

learned and sincere parliamentary body can find a way that will enable our society to move forward unafraid of more sophisticated knowledge, technology and challenges to the wonder of human procreation.
Recent landmark cases make clear the two sides of the ledger. On one side is the right to liberty, identified with human dignity and autonomy and the right to make fundamental personal decisions without state interference. On the other side, with as much validity is the public interest in the protection of the unborn. The Supreme Court has noted that there is a point at which the state interest in the protection of the foetus becomes compelling and responsibility for this protection falls to the legislature.
Let me remind this place once more of this additional burden. The most recent Supreme Court decision makes it very clear. It is this House and this House alone that holds "concern for the life of the foetus" in the cradle of its power to legislate.
I hold the current legislation up to the light of Northrop Frye's ledger and I examine its bottom line, as our current government likes to say so often. What angers me today is the lack of leadership and balance in this legislation. Bill C-43 clearly does not balance the beliefs, the fears and the genuine desires of Canadians. It is a mask of compromise rather than a genuine effort to integrate the two legitimate yet conflicting arguments on abortion. It declares abortion illegal in its text and then its qualifiers make abortion available virtually without restriction.
In the letter of the law it claims concern for the foetus and in its spirit it provides no protection for the foetus whatsoever. It unfairly places the full burden of responsibility on medical practitioners. From the mother's point of view, it makes a woman dependent on the idiosyncrasies of local community and provincial power structures.
Whatever balance the government claims it has established, it is an illusion. There is no evidence in this legislation that the public's concern for the welfare of the foetus has been addressed. This public concern which has clearly not been abandoned even by the Supreme Court of Canada, this other side of the ledger which must be balanced with the woman's right to individual choice, has not been given any sort of strength
Government Orders
in this sly piece of legislation. Although the government will claim it is sufficient that abortion remains in the Criminal Code and that this context is enough evidence of concern for the unborn, this too is mere posturing rather than substantial recognition of public concern for the foetus.
The Minister of Justice has stood in this place and said that Bill C-43 creates a criminal offence. Then, soon after, he informed news reporters that the government was not going to prosecute. This is hypocritical legislation. The presence of this new legislation in the Criminal Code in no way provides a reasonable balance of public desire on the issue of abortion. It gives the impression of concern for the foetus without the substance of enforceable law.
I call upon this government to provide legislation that is truly a compromise and that addresses both sides of the ledger clearly and effectively. Even as I call for changes in this legislation, it strikes me how narrow and limited this approach to child birth and the renewal of generations will be.
How can we ask women to carry new life to fruition unless we are prepared to provide the social environment and social vision that value new life clearly and pragmatically? As long as this government continues to cut back on social support systems, to dare tear down the universal social welfare programs, and is more concerned for dollars than for people, women will be uncertain of wearing the mantle of child birth.
Who are we as legislators to speak on the issue of abortion unless we are prepared to take better responsibility for the basics of new life-food, clothing, shelter and child care? Yet this government has put the infamous deficit ahead of these essentials at every turn in its legislative agenda.
Can women really believe that this government cares deeply for the birth of another child? Can we really believe that this government has a commitment to families, to those who most need assistance in raising children? Let us not be foolish enough to believe that this legislation does anything to enhance the quality of life in our community. Let us instead demand that the government stop its obsession with the market-place and

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
its financial ledgers and turn its attention to the far more important ledger of social needs and responsibility.
In closing, I am prepared to take this government at its word only when I see it is practising this concern in its legislation for social support systems. When the government begins to take seriously the cries for child care, the desperate need for more shelter, more clothing, more food, the responsibility to assist the provinces in providing a better quality of life for the poor and the unemployed, then and only then will Canadians believe that this legislation grows out of true concern for the lines of women and children.
As it stands this legislation is an abdication of responsibility. It has failed to balance the public's concern for the unborn child with the need to assure the dignity and rights of women. It is, above all, promulgated by a government whose whole legislative agenda devalues those very universal social programs which guarantee quality of life for all children.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, as introduced by my hon. colleague, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada.
Our government was faced with finding a solution to a problem that touches the very core of the basic values of Canadian men and women. As with any legislation where personal attitudes and moral convictions are involved, we could expect a lack of consensus within our own society. We can make this a legal debate. We can make this a matter of conscience. We can make this a scientific debate. The fact remains that although it may be difficult to accept, abortion is a reality. We must therefore give it a legislative framework that gives women the right to use their own judgment, that offers women a measure of protection and finally, that is aimed at preventing abuse. It is in this perspective that the legislator tabled this Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I speak first of all as a member of this House and as such, I support the decision of a responsible government to deal with a difficult and emotionally charged situation.
A legal vacuum was created, when the Supreme Court concluded that Section 251 of the Criminal Code was
contrary to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It was therefore up to the government to remove this contradiction by introducing legislation adapted to our times. The bill tabled in the House on November 3 is the result of solid thinking and reflects the wisdom of a government that is firm, fair and realistic.
If we look at the theoretical aspect, the legislation may seem inadequate. It is true that the subject is so emotionally charged that it creates controversy and makes discussion very difficult. However, the legislator was able to maintain the clarity and perspective required to consider the practical aspects and make abortion a medical act, subject to the rules of the profession: an act that arises from a decision made by a woman and her physician.
In tabling this bill, the government decided to avoid taking a stand for or against abortion, restricting its involvement to creating an objective framework for the act, which so far remains the best solution.
Second, I speak to you as a woman who, like many others, has acquired a measure of experience both in her personal and professional life.
Like any human being, I debate issues with myself and this helps me shape my opinions. I too have my own values and personal convictions and sometimes I call them into question when faced with realities that must ultimately be accepted.
Over the years, the status of women has evolved steadily in our society. Today we can say that women occupy a respectable place although they still have some obstacles to overcome.
Respect for personal choice is the very foundation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and all legislation must comply with it.
Abortion is not a choice between good and evil. A woman wants an abortion because she is tom inside; she sees it as a solution to a tragic situation.
Abortions, in many cases, result from a lack of external support and a feeling of rejection due to social prejudice. That is why I am convinced that the bill will enable a woman and her doctor to have a healthy dialogue. Together, they will have to decide how to deal with a problem which only they know in detail.
November 22, 1989

I am reassured by this legislation, Mr. Speaker, not only because it respects women's judgment but also because it protects them and is free of prejudice on an issue so closely related to social values.
I myself raised a family of four children. I was able to understand and intensely experience what motherhood and deciding to have a family mean for women. Based on this experience in my own family, I favour a situation and setting where women can develop and grow.
Society has evolved and so have women. Respecting women also means respecting their decisions, including what they do with their own bodies, in consultation with their doctor.
When I look at the past or compare us with the many countries to which my work takes me, countries which Canada helps, I say that Canadian society is doing more all the time for the equality of women in their individual and collective rights.
The bill before us today meets a basic need to respect individuals, to respect women and their decisions.
This respect, Mr. Speaker, must go together with our society's evolution, as women move towards greater autonomy. Will this bill settle everything? I sincerely do not think so. But that is no reason not to do something that will contribute to women's betterment and protect their basic right to decide with their doctors what is best for their physical and mental health.
If women have full rights in our society, legislators must be consistent with this great principle and enact it in legislation. This is just what we are doing today.
Mr. Speaker, as a woman and as a member of this House, I fully support the solution proposed in this bill. I recognize in it the leadership and tolerance which have guided our government throughout its term of office.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that everyone in this House has faced the same problem as I have in dealing with the abortion issue and now, more particularly, with Bill C-43.
As a new member of Parliament, I can safely say that this particular issue has dominated my mail. I must say
Government Orders
that I am pleased the matter is at least before the House so that we can finally deal with it and address the issue.
On a positive note, I think the bill has caused a great deal of hue and cry among the extreme positions on the issue. That, in itself, might be an endorsement for the bill. I believe that people in Canada are looking for an acceptable compromise, a compromise which deals with all sides of the issue and if you have both extremes upset, then maybe that is what this bill achieves, a compromise.
The Dodds and the Daigle cases this past summer have brought the issue home to millions of Canadians. It is an issue which affects everyone. I would hazard a guess that every member in this House knows of someone who has agonized over whether a person wanted or needed to have an abortion. It is an issue which affects all Canadians. Our role as legislators is to find a way to deal with this issue so that the constitutional rights of women are balanced with the rights of the foetus.
The question then becomes: "Does Bill C-43 achieve this objective?"
The bill is a negative bill, which neither protects the rights of the woman nor the rights of the foetus. The bill does not deal with many of the other surrounding issues involving this complex process, for I believe that we cannot just view this issue on the basis of abortion, but we must take a holistic point of view and abortion is really the final end of a very long and involved process.
As the Citizens for Public Justice said: "To introduce a pro-life amendment to the Criminal Code without social policy changes will not adequately protect human life. To give women legal right to abortion without social policy changes means that many women have few effective choices other than abortion. This is not a choice anyone would recommend."
In light of the recent decision in the Supreme Court of Canada, Daigle vs. Tremblay et al the court has found that under existing law the foetus has no rights until bom. I must say, as a lawyer reviewing the case, I can follow the logic of the decision and the conclusion, but I cannot agree with the conclusion in the sense that I feel that we, as legislators, must make the necessary changes and correct the results of the decision that has been reached by the Supreme Court of Canada. For this reason, I

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
would have preferred a degree of foetal protection in this bill. This bill does not provide that protection.
This bill basically is an amendment to the Criminal Code which makes all abortions criminal except in a case where a physician is of the opinion that the woman's physical, mental and psychological health is endangered by the continuance of the pregnancy. In any other circumstance, it is a criminal offence punishable by up to two years, imprisonment for anyone to induce an abortion, including self-inducement.
I must also say that I don't believe that women embark on the decision to have an abortion lightly. As a man I cannot say for sure because I won't have to face that decision, but it must be a hard, gut-wrenching decision, which in most circumstances appears to the woman involved as the only alternative available.
Looking at the bill, one quickly sees that it deals with the issues on a very negative basis and shifts responsibility for the decision. I do have some very grave hesitations with the criminalization of the mother, and I do not feel that the bill should shift that criminalization to the physician. The physician is now faced with a situation where he can make a decision or come to an opinion that an abortion is acceptable treatment and then be subject to prosecution at a later stage.
The provincial Attorney General or a Crown prosecutor may hold certain views which may start that process and leave that physician subject to criminal prosecution. As a lawyer, I would have to say that in most cases I would advise a physician never to do an abortion on the basis of the bill because of the vulnerability that the physician faces. While it would appear in the Supreme Court of Canada decision that third parties do not have any rights to bring actions, there is nothing to stop the criminal process from coming to the fore and for a Crown prosecutor or anyone to lay an information or start that process which is obviously bad for the physician.
The other problem which the physician faces is medical opinion across the country on what will be mental, physical or psychological health difficulties will differ in the different areas of Canada. I believe that the psychological definition is going to be the hardest one to come up with from a medical point of view and that definition
is not provided in the legislation. Therefore, a doctor is left to his own devices to define "psychological", and if he reaches the wrong conclusion could become a criminal.
Also, the bill does not provide equal access to women across the country. In effect, the legislation ducked that issue and put it in the hands of the provinces. Therefore, we will see unequal access to abortion across this country. We have seen that already under the existing law. In New Brunswick, for instance, there are regions within the province that perform abortions in certain hospitals and some that do not. We are going to exacerbate the situation by expanding that across the whole country with this type of legislation.
The Supreme Court of Canada in its decision said that foetal rights only arise once the foetus has been bom. This requires us as legislators to step in and resolve that problem to a degree in favour of the foetus. The Law Reform Commission had recommendations. I know that a lot of groups were opposed to those recomendations but at least it provided a degree of recognition of the rights of women and the rights of the foetus. In my view, in this legislation neither rights have been protected.
The legislation by its negative effect also causes the woman, in effect, to lie. She must go to the physician if she wants an abortion and concoct a story. That is exactly what has happened in the past and that is again a most unreasonable way for us to force women to act.
As I indicated earlier, I believe that we have to look at this issue from a holistic point of view. To bring forward legislation which just deals with abortion and does not deal with the other sides of the issue is a very negative way to proceed.
A classic case that we see in society today is children having children. How do we deal with that situation? An abortion is the last part of that whole process. We have an obligation to look at day care, to look at the opportunities that are presented, to look at family planning and those associated issues, and to deal with things like sex education and contraception when dealing with younger women. The issue is not just one of abortion. All issues such as family, day care, and reproductive technology are involved and should be associated with this particular bill. For us to come forward with legislation which only
November 22, 1989

deals with one aspect is shirking our responsibility as legislators.
My view is that at this particular stage we really do not have any choice but to send this bill to committee, hope for some amendments that will put some of the things that each one of us believe are necessary into the legislation, and hopefully fashion a piece of legislation which does the job rather than leaving it the way it is now. At this particular stage, we must send it to committee. Hopefully we can come up with amendments, but I must say that if the bill comes back in its present form, I would have no choice but to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-43, and I hope that my comments will be useful to the legislator and to this country. My presentation will reflect my experience in the practice of psychology. I will deal with three points in the few minutes at my disposal.
First, I will explain my position on the issues and the bill before the House today. Second, I intend to discuss the duality and apparent contradiction between the individual and society. Finally, I will discuss an approach that in my view would make it possible to enforce the legislation with a heightened understanding for the new realities in our society.
Let me say, first of all, that I believe in life. I will not try to determine whether the foetus is a human being, and I will not agonize about the exact moment when the foetus is considered to be a human being.
My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) raised the subject on Wednesday, November 8, at page 5725 in Hansard.
As was said before in the House, the purpose of this bill is to make abortion a medical act. This position is fundamental, and I welcome it. It is based on a definition of health, either mental, physical or psychological, and this definition is set within a social context. Mr. Speaker, the bill recognizes that the living foetus is not just an excrescence or a fibroma but quite definitely something different. I call this foetus a human being.
Government Orders
The Bill acknowledges this as well, since it is based on three guiding principles, the first of which is to balance the constitutional rights of the woman and society's interest in the protection of the foetus.
This principle indicates, in no uncertain terms, that abortion is not solely a private matter. It is also a matter that affects society and the public interest and hence it is a matter of ethics, whether social or religious or both.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) raised this question in the House and gave us an excellent answer. It seems almost impossible to dissociate social ethics from religious ethics. It is not any easier to dissociate the human spirit from its physiological counterpart.
Both Hippocrates and the philosophers acknowledged this fact. The modem scientist is no exception. The laws of nature, when they apply, always do so in a tangible, material world. Our laws are implicit in the matter that surrounds us. This is an accepted fact in both psychology and management.
The Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada said, and I quote:
In a perfect world, abortion would not be necessary for any
reason. We all know, however, that the world is not perfect.
We are human beings. We are finite beings, limited by our physiological and neurological equipment, and obviously will be for a number of centuries to come. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said there were few, if any, moral issues on which people agreed. He added that abortion was a disturbing issue for each and everyone of us because it seemed to force us to chose between two essential human values.
Mr. Speaker, no man is an island. He lives in an environment and belongs to a group. Therefore, he cannot make laws to please himself. That is why it is up to the legislator, with all his perfections and imperfections, to identify and implement standards. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I don't think this legislation is intended to let everyone do as they please or that it is a lawyer's paradise or that it puts the onus on the physician. In my view, people who say this are avoiding the issue.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to my second point. This bill merely recognizes two realities which exist whether we like it or not.

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
First, we have a woman. Second, this woman is carrying a foetus, a new being; she is no longer alone with her body. For this reason, she must deal with another reality called society.
In fact, two human beings form the basis of society. At the very least, they often provide all the elements needed to form a society, whether it is a cell, a group, a family.
We all know that living in a group or society raises many problems. Where does the freedon of one person begin and end and conversely where does the freedon of another person begin and end? Social psychology and the question it raises shed some light on this for us. Many say that this bill is aiming for a compromise. I do not think so. As I see it, the bill sets a standard for an inherent human problem: individual versus collective rights. In other words, the bill sets parameters so that two separate but interconnected entities can function and develop as harmoniously as possible. The individual depends on the richness of the group in order to stand out and find a way to excel.
Just as man influences his environment, it shapes his behaviour as much as it does his opinions, beliefs, attitudes and especially values. But if a society is to continue to envolve, individuals must be able to continue to assimilate its basic values.
Therefore the human being is always guided by an individual and collective vector, and his behavioural patterns are inspired by social prescriptions which themselves are tinted by factors of levelling and individualization.
It is in that sense that the feeling of belonging takes a connotation of development. Apparent dissonances such as group/individual, security/accomplishment, and level-ling/individualization convey a message to the extent that one accepts that an individual alone cannot develop fully enough, or at least to the degree that his potential can be actualized.
What may seem to be theoretical, philosophical and useless in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is not really so because this problem underlies human, social and even moral values.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I am satisfied with this bill, even though we may always encounter vile men, weaker women and physicians without strong conscience.
Even so, it is up to the institutions to step in and steer them back towards justice and equity, while keeping in mind both the individual and the group to which he belongs and from which he seeks guidance to sustain his own legitimacy and sense of belonging.
Mr. Speaker, I said that one cannot be independent without first having been dependent, and that the more independent one is the more one has to acknowledge one's dependence on others. I am no exception.
In the riding of Outremont which I am honoured to represent in this House, I have the privilege of listening to a wide range of opinions, and I can say that we find there the normal array of different positions. I must keep that in mind. If the citizens of the riding of Outremont have that right, it logically follows that their right becomes my duty.
One last point before I conclude. A little over a year ago I said to a journalist who asked me where I stood with respect to the abortion issue that I was pro-life. I went on to say, and I quote the newspaper article: "If we want a society to develop, that takes individuals. We must plant our own maple trees and see that they reproduce".
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that since the bill deals with a medical act and opinion and since neither the doctor nor the woman has all the relevant scientific information, it would be worthwhile for them to get the support and advice of professionals who could show them how to make the best decision.
And moral and religious convictions will finalize this process. Mr. Speaker, I am pro-life but I also recognize life in society requires flexibility.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a sense of sadness that I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-43, a bill to recriminalize abortion in Canada.
January 29, 1988, was an historic day not just for Canadian women but indeed for all Canadians. It was on that date that the Supreme Court of Canada struck down the criminal provisions dealing with abortion in a decision which stated that they were in breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
November 22, 1989

Madam Justice Bertha Wilson, in her very eloquent reasons for judgment, stated that the right to reproduce or not to reproduce, which is an issue in this case is one such right under section 7 and is properly perceived as an integral part of modern women's struggle to assert her dignity and worth as a human being. Judge Wilson went on to state that section 251 treated women as a means, a means to an end which she does not desire but over which she has no control. She is the passive recipient of a decision made by others as to whether her body is to be used to nurture a new life.

Mr. Speaker, Chief Justice Brian Dickson, in his judgment on the Morgentaler case, said that forcing a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she met some criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations is a profound interference with her body and thus violates security of the person.

In striking down the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with abortion, the court recognized a number of very serious flaws in that legislation, flaws which frequently led to delays that put women at risk and increased the risk of complication. Indeed, Canada had the second highest rate of mid-trimester abortions of all industrialized nations. The requirements for therapeutic abortion committees clearly led to the kind of delays that, in turn, resulted in complications which could lead to health problems for Canadian women.
In addition, too often in this country we have seen destructive battles for the control of hospital boards based solely on the question of abortion because of deeply held feelings on the part of both those who oppose abortion and those who are in support of freedom of choice. Instead of hospital boards which are elected to deal with a whole range of health care concerns, under the old legislation we had hospital boards which too often were driven in a harsh and unrealistic way to respond only on this issue.
I want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the dedication and the commitment of many women and men across this land in the struggle that culminated in the great victory for women on January 29, 1988 when
Government Orders
the criminal law with respect to abortion was struck down.
I remember the role played by Grace Mclnnis. Grace Mclnnis, a former New Democratic Party Member of Parliament, served this country with distinction in a whole range of areas, was the only woman in the House of Commons who, when the provisions on the Criminal Code were adopted, stood up with dignity and courage and called for this decision to be left to a woman and her doctor, outside the purview of criminal law.
I think of my very distinguished predecessor as the spokesperson on justice for the New Democratic Party, Stuart Leggatt, now a judge in British Columbia, who fought long and hard to establish this principle. Many of my colleagues in the House today, and I single them out in particular, one being the spokesperson on the status of women, my colleague for Vancouver East has struggled so long, not just for freedom of choice, but for real alternatives for Canadian women to help reduce the number of abortions in Canada.
I think of the women from across this land who have struggled to establish free standing clinics to provide women with access to safe therapeutic abortions, Every Woman's Health Clinic in Vancouver, a clinic in Winnipeg, in Toronto, and those women who are seeking to establish a clinic in Halifax.
I think of Dr. Henry Morgentaler. Dr. Morgentaler has waged a battle of courage, integrity and in some cases doing time in jail to stand up for the right of Canadian women to make this basic decision for themselves.
I think of Chantal Daigle, a young woman from Quebec whose personal life was dragged across the front pages of the newspapers and television, and who was the victim of an act of judicial violence in my view by the Quebec Court of Appeal. I was in the Supreme Court of Canada for the hearings and I rejoiced when the Supreme Court reversed that decision of the Quebec Court of Appeal, that decision which allowed her boyfriend to tell her that she could not make this very difficult and agonizing decision for herself and who had admitted that, yes, he had beaten her but he had not left any marks.
Many of us had hoped that this government would recognize that instead of bringing forward new criminal legislation, what was needed were changes to Canada's health legislation to ensure equitable access across this

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
country and concrete measures to reduce unwanted pregnancies, and to assist women who want to keep their children but who, in many cases, are faced with a crushing burden of poverty.
That was not to be so. What did this bill do? While the Supreme Court of Canada in its judgment on Chantal Daigle has closed the door on civil injunctions, this Conservative government has opened the door to criminal prosecution of both women and their doctors. We in the New Democratic Party find that deeply offensive and we reject categorically recriminalization of abortion in this land.
Let us be very clear on this. This has been a long standing policy of the New Democratic Party. It is with considerable sadness that I have listened this evening to representatives from the Liberal party, including the associate critic on justice who indicated that they will be supporting this bill at second reading and agreeing to the recriminalization of abortion. Indeed, it is not surprising, given the fact that the Liberal leader himself in August of this year urged the government to bring forward new criminal legislation.
In introducing this legislation, the Minister of Justice has said that he has confidence in Canadian doctors and Canadian women. If he has confidence in Canadian doctors and Canadian women, and indeed he should, he should recognize that there is no need for new criminal legislation. Instead, we should be moving to ensure under the Canada Health Act access for women across this land. This bill does nothing whatsoever to assist those women in Prince Edward Island who were denied access; to assist the women in Newfoundland who have but a single doctor in St. John's, and when that doctor is sick or on holidays, they must travel to Montreal or elsewhere.

Mr. Speaker, this bill does nothing at all for women who, in many regions of Quebec, have no abortion service and often Quebec women must travel hundreds of miles to large centres; some hospitals refuse abortions for married women or those who do not use the pill or contraceptive devices.
So we should be looking at access and we should be looking, fundamentally, at alternatives. Instead of cutting back on funding for the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada, we should be increasing funding, looking into the whole question of child poverty, into research into safe and effective contraception, to the removal of workplace and environmental reproductive hazards, to care for pregnant women and new mothers, to access to reproductive health services, including abortion services.
In closing, I want to say that these are the issues which we in the New Democratic Party believe should be addressed by this government. Every child must be a wanted child. Yes, I am pro-life. I support the life of those children in our society who are too often victims of poverty, the 150,000 children that line up at food banks every day. I deeply reject the suggestions that somehow we in the New Democratic Party are not in support of life. Indeed, too often those who attack us are concerned about life which starts at conception, but their concern ends at the birth of the child. I want to say that we reject the recriminalization of abortion in Canada and we appeal to this government to take steps to ensure that Canadian children live a life in which they are wanted and in which they do not live in poverty and that Canadian women are allowed to make this very basic and fundamental decision for themselves in consultation with their doctors.

Mr. Speaker, since Bill C-43 has been made public most of us, I believe, have received considerable numbers of letters from constituents and from interested Canadians in all parts of the country.
It is interesting to note for the record that for completely different reasons we have received and continue to receive correspondence that expresses on the part of the writers a view against the bill. The view is expressed by those who belong to the pro-life movement, as well as by those who are on the pro-choice side of the issue. That fact creates a dilemma for the legislators. When you have two very articulate groups of citizens expressing their views on a very important social issue, it is then left, I suppose, to each one of us to draw our own conclusions as to what course of action to take
November 22, 1989

in an attempt to reflect as well as we can the views of our constituents. Believe me, this breakdown into two streams of correspondence in the mail makes the task arduous.
Nobody likes and nobody wants abortion. And at the same time, nobody wants to treat the mother as if she has no rights from the moment she becomes pregnant. There are rights that have to be taken into account for both the unborn and the mother. And one, I submit to you, does not exclude the other.
Therefore, if you approach the issue from this point then inevitably the legislators have to address the question of demand for abortion. It must be addressed in a manner so as to reduce the demand for abortion by approaching what I would describe the large middle ground of this issue between pro-life and pro-choice ideologies. There is a significant and very important middle ground.
I submit to you that it is not an either/or question. The question is how to deal with the situation so as to reduce as much as possible the demand for abortion and possibly eliminate it. The question is how to reduce the demand.
That subject has been developed in a four-pronged approach. It begins with education of the population at large by way of family planning and by way of education on contraception.
Second, it means dealing with young people providing them with a better teacher than just the experience of life. It means an understanding of how reproduction works, how the human body works and how to prevent the pregnancy.
Third, we come to the important aspect of the involvement of man. As we all know, no woman has made herself pregnant alone. Therefore, man should and must be helped to recognize his equal responsibility in all aspects of sexuality. In terms of decision making, he must be helped to recognize his responsibility also in obtaining and using contraception and also his equal responsibility in the handling of crisis when it occurs.
We must be perfectly clear that there is a desperate need in our society for support services. This issue cannot be treated in isolation from the vacuum that exists today in terms of support services. Therefore, the debate on the question of abortion must focus principally on this question. You need to have social and economic
Government Orders
measures in place in the form of programs. And they must be available to people whether they are rich or poor. In specific terms they have to touch on housing, day care, counselling and on post-natal employment. The fact which has been brought to the attention of all parliamentarians over the years on a number of occasions is that poverty has been found to be one of the strongest reasons for abortion. That fact must be addressed.
I have outlined for you in the limited time available this four-pronged approach which, to my way of understanding the issue, is an essential policy that is needed if we are to discuss in an intelligent manner the question respecting abortions.
I am indebted to the British Columbia Teachers' Status of Women Journal of June of 1988 for having produced these elements. We must also ask ourselves what would be achieved by outlawing abortions. Would it prevent abortions, or would that drive those wanting abortions underground and make the practice one that is still with us but not necessarily in a visible form? The polarization of this issue is a matter of serious concern, and as parliamentarians it seems to me that we should resist stressing what divides us on this issue and stress instead what brings us together on a social issue of such importance.
We must, therefore, identify the viable solutions of this matter. Why create a conflict, I ask you? Why sharpen it? Why not instead diffuse it where possible and to the largest possible degree?
A lot has been said on Bill C-43. I wanted to put on record some views. I must tell you that in the knowledge I have of this bill tonight, if a vote were to take place, I would find it necessary to vote against it because I find it inadequate.

Mr. Speaker, while it may be difficult, if not impossible for me to offer any new perspective or original thought on the subject of abortion after the many thousands of words which have been spoken previously on this subject in this House, nevertheless, I do value this opportunity to express my own views about the issue, both in terms of my personal convictions as an individual and of my legislative responsibilities as a Member of Parliament.

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
In fact, I think it is extremely important to note these two very distinct aspects to the role of all hon. members in considering this matter of abortion. Perhaps it is only such a rare issue which is so unique to itself. Those considerations are not only how we feel about abortion within our own minds and consciences but also how we view our responsibilities as elected representatives to consider abortion on behalf of society, to reflect the common interest, to lead public opinion, to bring order out of confusion and, in short, to provide good government with respect to this most difficult subject.

Mr. Speaker, I found that abortion is more than a difficult issue. For me, it shows the very need for a government decision. I personally have not only the problem of reconciling my own ideas with those of my constituents but also my great priority of helping create a law for good government. But in fact, in Canada, our constituents are extremely divided. According to the best estimates, approximately 20 per cent are truly opposed to abortion, another 20 per cent are for free choice and about 60 per cent are in between these two extremes.

To add further complexity to the decision which I and each one of us must make is the fact that the Supreme Court has struck down existing laws concerning abortion and since that has happened in the vacuum of any effective federal law, there have been lower court judgments in various parts of Canada which have brought sharply conflicting rulings and which have, over the past several months, created a sad spectacle of social confusion, intrusion of privacy, and embarrassment of individuals, all into full public view on our television screens.
There is little wonder then that in this House of Commons we are facing a continuing dilemma of a clear need to create law governing abortion and to provide legal and ethical guidelines for Canadian society. Yet being frustrated by the experience of the last Parliament, when I understand this House was unable to gain a majority on any one of a combination of resolutions and amendments put before it about abortion, it is in this context about an issue bearing all of the agonizing characteristics to be the most extreme of political considerations, that the government recently invited a number of caucus members to grapple with the subject to seek a
resolution that would meet the test of three imperatives. First, a resolution that would be in the form of a law adequate to provide a clear legal and ethical reference for all Canadians. Second, a resolution that would receive the approval of this House of Commons by way of at least majority voting support by its members. Third, a resolution that would, in all likelihood, prove stable against any appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
As one of those caucus members invited to participate in these discussions, I feel it is worthwhile to share with all of my colleagues and my constituents the process of considerations which we pursued in arriving at, for the most part reluctantly I should say, the consensus which is generally reflected in the content of Bill C-43 now before us. Represented in the composition of our group was the complete range of views that undoubtedly exist among hon. members and, in fact, among Canada's population about the abortion issue, from strong antiabortion convictions on the one hand to equally strong freedom-of-choice positions on the other, and with a spectrum of moderate views between those two extremes.
Convictions and positions were not easily sacrificed in the search for consensus. But as our discussions intensified to meet these three essential criteria, a gradual movement emerged toward the higher level of our responsibilities as legislators and to the compelling objective of creating a law to govern abortion that would meet all the tests. What we have arrived at, as expressed in Bill C-43, is a consensus that represents, as I have said previously, the true essence of politics, "The art of the possible", with respect to abortion.
There was full accord that a law governing abortion was an essential requirement for Canadian society. But it was not possible to reach accord in total opposition to abortion and it was not possible to reach accord in support for complete freedom of choice. This Bill C-43 was not the original position nor even the first consensus choice of the participants. Eventually, it did emerge as the one statement which we have come to believe will best provide a legal framework for a national position on abortion, while at the same time winning a majority support in the House of Commons to become law, and having the most likelihood to successfully withstand appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada.
November 22, 1989

This position was reached only after long and intense debate and only with politically responsible reflection on the part of virtually all members involved. I would readily call it a consensus but I would hesitate to describe it as a compromise in the traditional sense of that word, because it does express some important principles which make it, in my view, a distinctive and contemporary Canadian legal statement.
What does Bill C-43 really say? Well, for me, it clearly seems to say several important things. First, it says that abortion is fundamentally illegal in Canada and that protection of the foetus from conception until birth is a basic priority. It says that the health of the mother is also a priority, be it physical, mental or psychological and may take precedence over the foetus if judged to be necessary in the opinion of the woman's doctor.
It does not purport to render a decision about the legality of any specific abortion, but rather places the onus for that judgment in every case upon the doctor as he or she may be licensed to practise medicine under the laws of each respective province. It says, by implication, that the selection and approval of facilities where an abortion may be performed will similarly be at the judgment of the doctor within generally accepted standards of the medical profession in the province or provinces in which the doctor is licensed to practise. It also seems to say by implication that the payment of medicare benefits for abortion procedures will be in accordance with federal-provincial medicare agreements within the province or provinces in which the doctor is licensed to practise medicine and in which the abortion is carried out.
In terms of the broad public debate with which the abortion issue has been seized over the past many months, Bill C-43 does implicitly address the value and dignity of life, both of the foetus and of the mother. As proposed, Bill C-43 clearly states the principle of protection of the foetus from the moment of conception until birth. It does so by making it illegal to induce an abortion unless the mother's health is threatened. It also does so by excluding any reference to a gestational period of time. Therefore, I believe that Bill C-43 does clearly state fundamental respect for life from conception which
Government Orders
is a deeply held conviction for a large number of Canadians, perhaps for most of us.
At the same time, Bill C-43 recognizes the priority of the woman's own health and her right to obtain an abortion if her health is threatened either physically, mentally or psychologically. I realize that this is a broad definition of health, subject to the professional opinion of the woman's doctor, and in practical terms will ensure that abortion is accessible on a reasonable and equitable basis for all women where it is required.
Essentially, the proposed law recognizes that abortion is a medical decision and places the onus for that decision on the qualified medical opinion of the doctor in consultation with the woman. The criminal responsibility for abortion decisions has been transferred from the woman to the doctor.
I think it is worth stating that even in so-called circumstances of free choice, the woman ultimately would have to gain the approval of a doctor to have the abortion. So freedom of choice is never really absolute. Also I have become convinced that most of those who support freedom of choice as a right do not necessarily or even generally support abortion as a principle.
Considering all of these factors, I remain convinced that Bill C-43 is the best possible resolution and perhaps the only right one for this very difficult issue. Not only do I feel that way because it is my first duty as a parliamentarian to help create an effective law on this subject but, coincidentally, Bill C-43 as it is now proposed does reasonably reflect my own moderate position on the matter as I have previously and consistently expressed in public.
Perhaps my previous views bear repeating at this time. I would like to say that one year ago during the election campaign of 1988 I expressed the view that abortion was a difficult decision to be made by a woman in consultation with her doctor. If the question arose in my own daughter's case, I would encourage her to bear the child. Ultimately, however, I would be prepared to accept her decision with love and respect, whatever that decision might be, subject to the professional opinion of her doctor.
In closing, we as parliamentarians and legislators must address ourselves to a consensus which will provide for most Canadians some basis for social order and tolerance among conflicting views, if not for reconciliation of

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
those views. I believe that over time Bill C-43 will prove to fulfil such purposes and I encourage all hon. members to give it their support.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased this evening to be able to address the House on the subject of Bill C-43.1 think it is fair at the outset to indicate to the House that I do not feel I can support this bill.
