The main reason is that I do not believe the bill accomplishes the goal that I think it should have set out to achieve. It uses the same framework as the previous abortion legislation contained in the Criminal Code before the Morgentaler decision. That old framework, going back many years, in which our society attempted to prohibit or curtail abortions, was based on what I think history shows was a profound ignorance of what happened inside the womb.
The generations which preceded us had very little knowledge of the intricacies of child development in the womb and afterward for that matter. As a result they tried to resolve the messy problem of abortion by targeting the mother and the abortionist. At this stage in our history I do not believe that we have any more excuses. We have no excuses not to recognize precisely what happens in the womb and the various stages of development of life.
It is my view that we should not be prohibiting abortions based on who the mother is, or who the father is, or who the doctor is, or what they think at the time. We should be dealing with the issue of abortion because of who the foetus is. I want to suggest that the foetus, this will not surprise anyone here, is in fact the genesis of all human life. It is the genesis of all of mankind here on the planet today. I believe in our society what this government should be recognizing is that genesis of life and the protection to which it should be entitled.
We continue to learn more every day about how life is formed and how the human body takes shape. The study of genetics is a major field of study and experimentation today. I believe that that particular field of study is related to the way in which we deal with the issue of abortion. I am not suggesting that a statute or a bill proposal now would be able to deal with all of the issues.
I recognize that a royal commission has been created for the purpose of studying several of those issues.
I do fear how our society will deal with issues such as the human mutant, created unintentionally or intentionally, and I believe that that issue should be dealt with in the same framework as the human foetus should be treated in our law. I believe that all of our laws should reflect this and I believe that our Charter should reflect this. The use of the Criminal Code to deal with protection of the foetus is anachronistic and it is based on ignorant concepts of just how human life begins.
I believe our law should be protecting the foetus. However, the current proposal does only two things. First, it sets out to criminalize the conduct of a mother, or a doctor, or an abortionist, and then it creates an exception to that criminalization, which really provides in the end result no protection to the foetus. Last, the bill fails to articulate for society the role of society in ensuring that birthing and parenting are properly regarded as essential elements in the health and well-being of our country. I do not believe that removing the foetus from the womb at any stage and disposing of the foetus as we customarily dispose of our normal refuse accomplishes any of these goals for our society and I think it is crucially important that we recognize this at this stage of our history.
I feel that with this bill, I and that portion of humanity which may still be in the womb are still awaiting a bill which will accomplish these goals.

Madam Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to address Bill C-43 on abortion. This is a matter that is extremely difficult for me because I feel it is very personal for each individual and that I should not be advancing my own views on this issue. At the same time it is important to relay my constituents' views on issues of their concern and this is the first occasion to convey those concerns on abortion.
Allow me to present three aspects: First, an overview of Bill C-43 as we understand it; second, some concerns that arise therefrom and third, my own position regarding BiU C-43.
This is indeed a controversial issue but we need legislation without further delay. This proposed legislation pays heed to the Supreme Court's opinion on abortion. In the January 1988 decision the Supreme Court of Canada reminded us as federal law makers that any policy or law on abortion, first, could not deny a
November 22, 1989

woman fair and reasonable access to abortion, second, must protect the woman's constitutional right to security of the person and, third, would reflect the state's interest in the foetus. Finally, it would have to protect the woman's life.
Bill C-43 achieves all of these objectives to some extent in its attempt to accommodate both sides of the debate. Unfortunately it will not be possible to satisfy both sides. The Supreme Court also recommended that Parliament secure a medically sound opinion as to the meaning of life or health. The proposed legislation now provides a definition as to the meaning of health. Section 287(2) states that health includes, for greater certainty, physical, mental and psychological health. Perhaps consideration ought to be given to a more narrow definition, to help define mental and psychological or, in the alternative, certain guidelines could be included for the doctor to use in his assessment process.
This bill reflects the fundamental belief that abortion is a medical act, one that requires consultation between a woman and her doctor so that valid health grounds can be established, thereby respecting society's interest in a foetus. However, this may give a doctor an absolute discretion in making a decision. It is his opinion that is decisive to the issue of termination of pregnancy.
Opinion has been defined in Section 287(2) as an opinion formed using generally accepted standards of the medical profession. It is unclear, however, what generally accepted standards of the medical profession are and who will overlook the medical doctors' practices to ensure these standards are being adhered to.
There is no enforcement mechanism or review of this opinion. If a review of doctors' practices were put in place perhaps the interests of the unborn would be better protected. Some have argued that the unborn is protected by the criminal sanction imposed but this is after the fact. There does appear a need for clearer guidelines to be given to the doctor so he can carry out the intention of Parliament, which is to achieve a balance.
If I may digress for a moment to a personal perspective, as a native Indian my upbringing has had a significant bearing on my own views of life. We view life in all forms to be very important. Human life is to be ho-
Govemment Orders
noured and respected as a gift of the great spirit. It is a gift for which we are to be very thankful.
In conclusion, although it does not fully protect the unborn, the passage of this bill at second reading is imperative. It is imperative so that we are all afforded the opportunity to move to committee where I hope to see more clarification or improvement in substance.
Therefore my position, one of pro-life, is to support passage of Bill C-43 at second reading. We need legislation with which to work and I look forward to amendments that may improve the proposed legislation. The full process of Parliament must be executed for this very vital issue.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak against this bill. It is a bill that is wrong in principle and it is a bill that will be hurtful in practice. I believe very strongly that in the final analysis the decision to terminate a pregnancy or, to put it the other way around, the decision to carry a baby to term, must be that of the woman alone. For the state to interfere with that decision is profoundly wrong in principle. For that to be adopted by this House, an overwhelming case in principle and in practice must be made, and no such case has been made.
I address the House as a New Democrat. Our party's position is clear. Our leader last night put our position on record very eloquently. I speak as a Canadian and as a father. I believe that life is sacred and that we must treat life with great respect, but I believe that this bill does not do so, that this bill will not protect unborn babies or the foetus. This is a bill, to put it very bluntly, which is designed to protect politicians.
I speak as a Christian. I believe that life is the gift of God. But I believe in the final analysis that the complex decision that must take place in balancing the act of creation with the reality of creation must be made by the woman. That decision cannot be made by a doctor, that decision cannot be made by parliamentarians, that decision cannot be made by lawyers or judges. It must be made in the final analysis by the woman involved and it will be made by the woman involved whatever law this House adopts.
Canadians have varying degrees of views on what is moral in this area of abortion. Some would say, as we have heard in the House so far, that virtually no abortion could be described as moral. Others would accept it perhaps in the case of rape or incest; others would say if the life of the woman is endangered; others would say if the health of the woman is endangered. That decision about health can be defined in different ways; physical,

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
mental or psychological health. Others would say that it is moral to have an abortion if in the final decision that pregnancy would be unwanted. There are these different views and no law can capture that range of different moral views on this very difficult question.
This bill encapsulated one view which is that it is moral to have an abortion if the health of the mother, as defined by physical, mental or psychological health, is at risk. But that is not a view which is universally shared in this country. Therefore, apart from anything else, this bill will not work. It is wrong in principle and it will be wrong and hurtful in practice.
The church to which I belong, the Anglican Church of Canada, has spoken out on this issue. Many faithful Anglicans have taken different positions. The church itself is, as it describes it, cautiously in favour of the bill. In my view that position is wrong, and the reservations which the Anglican Church has are more powerful than the reasons it advances for the bill.
Let me deal with a series of specific flaws in this bill. First, it reverses the onus. It says than an abortion is unlawful unless certain circumstances are met. That puts the onus on the defendant to show that the defendant is not guilty of an offence.
Second, by having the law turn on the opinion of a doctor the bill then becomes open to challenge from every kook and every nut who wants to challenge the individual decision of that doctor. Every doctor is going to have a somewhat different view of what is involved in the medical health of the mother in a particular case. Not only do we have a law which is open to challenge from whoever chooses to challenge it, but we also have a law which will be widely inconsistent in application. A law which is inconsistent in application is a bad law.
There is no requirement in this law that where an abortion is lawful a hospital must perform it. There is no guarantee of access to a lawful abortion and that is why the Supreme Court struck down the other law. This law will not stand the test which is why I say again it is a law
not to protect the foetus, it is a law to protect politicians who must band together to try to fend off attack.
This is an occasion not for compromise on principle, this is an occasion for a principal decision by each individual legislator in this House. This bill offends the decision of the Supreme Court in Canada by making abortions in the early terms of pregnancy illegal in certain circumstances. It alters the doctor-patient relationship. In every other case the doctor offers an opinion to the patient and the patient decides in the final analysis whether to accept the treatment and the recommendation of the doctor. This turns that relationship on its head. It puts the doctor in the controlling position. Doctors in this country should be standing up in force against this legislation and this House should not put doctors in this position.
This bill invites doctor shopping. There will become known in the community doctors who take a broad view of the language of this bill. There will be doctors who take a narrow view. In communities where there is only one doctor, who may take a very narrow view, women will be deprived of a right which they have in other communities of Canada.
Finally, this bill fails to meet one of the underlying fundamental requirements of any criminal law which is that it reflects the broad consensus in the society. There is no consensus around the moral provisions of this bill and that, among other reasons, is why the bill will fail.
I want to refer the House to the words of Madam Justice Wilson. She said:
This decision (of having an abortion) is one that will have profound psychological, economic and social consequences for the pregnant woman. The circumstances giving rise to it can be complex and varied and there may be, and usually are, powerful considerations militating in opposite directions. It is a decision that deeply reflects the way the woman thinks about herself and her relationship to others and to society at large. It is not just a medical decision; it is a profound social and ethical one as well. Her response to it will be the response of the whole person.
Those are wise words, Madam Speaker, words which this House must take into account. She said further on the question of religion and conscience:
Accordingly, for the state to take sides on the issue of abortion, as it does in the impugned legislation by making it a criminal offence for the pregnant woman to exercise one of her options, is not only to endorse but also to enforce, on pain of a further loss of liberty through actual

November 22, 1989

imprisonment, one conscientiously-held view at the expense of another. It is to deny freedom of conscience to some, to treat them as means to an end, to deprive them -of their "essential humanity". Can this comport with fundamental justice?
The way with which this issue of abortion must be dealt is not to put it back in the criminal law. The Supreme Court of Canada has now laid down the grounds that under existing law the foetus has no legal rights. The foetus may have moral rights. That is for each individual to determine. But the foetus has no legal rights and in that regime we can then move to begin truly to protect children in our society, to protect women in our society, to protect life in our society.

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
fellow citizens of social and medical services. I simply want to express my deep and personal conviction. I lived in Quebec during the 40s and 50s when the word was "believe or die", and in my pastoral activities, while promoting and suggesting the great values of the gospel to my congregation, I always tried to show tolerance and I was one of those who enjoyed meeting with divorced people, it did not matter to me. If you believe the lesson of the gospel, the Church welcomes you.
I think that as legislators in this House we ought to be tolerant. I am fully aware tonight that we must legislate within narrow limits for the Supreme Court would never accept a bill which would condemn abortion outright. This is something we must realize and tell our people. Otherwise, the Supreme Court would rule that such a bill goes against the right of women to the security of their person as was emphasized by Chief Justice Dickson. But there is the other side of the coin, the respect for life which is a real value, something which Justices Beetz and Wilson emphasized, adding that the interest of the state is to safeguard a minimum of control.
I feel, therefore, that Bill C-43 introduces an interesting element, the fact that the medical profession will have to decide. It is an interesting notion. Judging from a number of speeches here, I had the feeling that physicians are nothing but robots and automatons; yet, we are all well aware of the tact the Canadian Medical Association maintain very high standards and that most physicians I know are respectable people who do not decide lightly to carry out an operation, either to terminate a pregnancy or in any other area. I suggest that we should rely on the professional competence and quality of Quebec and Canadian practitioners. Whatever the position Parliament may adopt and it is a very pragmatic view, in my pastoral work I had personally to interview women who had decided to seek an abortion and I tried to reason with them, but when a woman has made up her mind, she will go ahead no matter what Parliament may decide. In this connection, a legislation which would be too stringent would favour affluent women and make it possible for those who can afford it, to have their pregnancies terminated wherever such services are available.
Therefore, we need a legislation which provides a balance between- A legislation is not an ideal in life. We are aware that the law forbids us to kill, but I wonder if life would be worth living if our purpose was simply not to kill at any cost. We are here to set up a framework within which the respect for life is proclaimed as a principle, abortion is forbidden unless a qualified physician agrees it is justified.
This being said, Madam Speaker, I would like in conclusion to make a very important point. It seems to me that the abortion legislation now before us must be examined in the light of the need for a much more comprehensive family policy. In that respect, I very much appreciated the speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who listed a number of projects that hopefully will be announced in the shortest possible timeframe to help enlighten Canadians. I am referring especially to young people. Of the 70,000 abortions performed each year in Canada, half involved women under 25. In that respect, whether in the area of family planning or tax measures for families on child care, I for one hope that we revive as soon as possible what we had on the Table before Parliament was dissolved before the election, so that families once more are given support and that we go to the root of the problem. I cannot believe that there is a single Canadian woman were she to enjoy physical and psychological health, and financial means, who would even accept to have her pregnancy terminated. It is my hope that this government will compliement this abortion legislation with a series of measures to ensure that families, pregnant women and girls can have all the financial, moral and psychological support they should expect from the state.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak again on this subject, having spoken on it just about 18 months ago. I would like to make several points that are important to me and I think maybe are important to a broad spectrum of our society.
First, I would like to say that there are two reasons for this debate. The first is that any civilized society must make a statement about what it values the most, what is normal, what is orderly. If we are to be a civilized society, that is the nature of civilization. We speak to order, we speak to value, we speak to norms.
November 22, 1989

The legislation we are debating today prohibiting abortions except in certain circumstances is making a statement about life, it is making a statement about what is normal and wholesome and orderly, and it is doing it by implication because it does not address those factors. It is making a statement about sanctions. But in speaking to sanctions this bill is saying that in the ordinary course of things it is normal to give birth; it is extraordinary to ask for an abortion. It is normal to want to give life, it is normal to be exuberant at the thought of birth and exuberant at the thought of reproducing ourselves. That is normality. It is extraordinary to have an abortion. In fact, the Supreme Court itself in its language of January 1988 called abortion an extraordinary medical procedure.
We are dealing with sanctions. As in all of life, while we are permitted to do almost anything, the law speaks to those sanctions which we find repulsive and we will not tolerate in a civilized society. Because we are speaking to sanctions in this legislation it underscores the normal, the accepted, the value of life.
The second reason we are debating this bill now is because the Supreme Court has asked us to. It said in its Morgentaler decision that there are two important factors about abortion. One is the protection of women and the second is the protection of life. It threw out the old abortion legislation because it did not properly protect women. It needed to throw out that legislation because if women are to have protection it cannot be seen as being uneven across Canada. It cannot be arbitrary, nor can it be illusory. Therefore, the Supreme Court was absolutely correct in rejecting the former legislation.
In pronouncing its judgment it also asked Parliament, almost begged Parliament, to make a definition of the value of the foetus. I quote Justice Wilson on page 26 of her judgement as follows:
"I believe that the main objective advanced to justify a restriction on the pregnant woman's Section 7 right is the protection of the foetus. I think this is a perfectly valid legislative objective."
Justice Dickson in the majority decision states at page 38:
Government Orders
Like Beetz and Wilson, I agree that the protection of the foetal interests by Parliament is also a valid governmental objective. It follows that balancing these interests, with the lives and health of women a major factor, is clearly an important governmental objective.
Beetz goes on to state at page 43 of his judgment: "Accordingly I believe that the state's interest in protecting potential human life exists throughout pregnancy."
On page 4 he makes this statement: "The primary objective of Section 251 of the Criminal Code is the protection of the foetus. The protection of the life and health of a pregnant woman is an ancillary objective. The primary objective does relate to concerns which are pressing and substantial in a free and democratic society in which, pursuant to Section 1 of the charter, justify reasonable limits to be put on a woman's right."
The Supreme Court has asked us to make a statement about worth. This legislation, by stating that the foetus deserves protection from conception to birth, makes a statement about worth of that foetus, of that unborn child.
It speaks to intrinsic worth. It does not depend on external factors like viability, or potential, or becoming a productive member of society. Those are externals. The worth of the unborn is intrinsic. It does not depend on those externals. Any gestational approach implies or suggests some level of expendability, a graduated level of worth.
Sooner or later, unfortunately, when we introduce those kinds of graduated values, it becomes reduced to an economic unit rather than the intrinsic value of becoming a productive member of society-will that person fit, will that person be able to earn a living, will that person be dependent? It comes down to economic values.
The irony is that for centuries women who have been angered at their subjugation at the hands of a male dominated society have rebelled against values that put extrinsic worth on them rather than intrinsic worth. For years they have tried to make the point, and have done it successfully, that they have value in themselves, not because they are housewives, lawyers, or doctors, but because they are people the way anyone else is.
If that is true for women, is that not true for the unborn? Should we perpetuate the notion that life has extrinsic value rather than intrinsic value?

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
This legislation is important because it states clearly that life is important from conception on, and everybody has worth regardless of the age at time of conception or time of senility. It is not the value we put on them that makes them valued.
It is time for us to be building an ethical climate that will provide security and sanctity for the unborn from the moment of conception.
I want to read, in closing, from an article in a publication entitled Christianity Today. It is an article written by Tim Stafford on October 6 in which he states, referring to Roe v. Wade, and I ask my colleagues to bear with me:
The discussion had been about where to draw the line among tragic choices; the justices erased the line completely and said there was no room for further discussion.
Anti-abortionists may someday have reason to remember this lesson, if they gain the power to stop abortion by fiat. As we have seen, restricting abortion works best when it is based on a wider consensus about the value of life. The first centuries of the church gained this consensus through centuries of witness. They spoke passionately against abortion as a part of their faith. They also suffered for their faith. Ultimately their faith triumphed and legal changes followed.
By contrast, the 19th centuiy though it passed anti-abortion laws seems not to have built a strong, public consciousness of the humanity of a foetus.
Ethicist Stanley Hauerwas touches on this issue when he notes the frustration of anti-abortionists who fail to convince their opponents that a foetus is a human being. He says that more than logic is needed and continues:
Christian arguments about abortion -have not merely failed to convince: they have failed to suggest the kind of "reorientation" necessary if we are to be the kind of people and society that make abortion unthinkable -Even if [we succeed politically!, our success may still be a form of failure if we "win" without changing the presuppositions of the debate.
That is what Christians in the first three centuries managed to do. They changed the world, not just the law.
I would say, Madam Speaker, to the many people out there who are concerned about this issue that we are facing an ethical morass more than a legal morass. I was watching television the other day and I heard Carmen McRae sing a song and the recurring line was: "Your gentle touch has made me strong".
I would say to those anti-abortionists out there who are carrying placards and chaining themselves to fences: put away the chains, put away the placards, and get a little closer to people. The confrontation separates us. If we could get close enough to embrace and to comfort,
rather than to confront, then maybe we could begin building the kind of an ethical consensus that would make a stronger abortion law possible and give the kind of protection to the unborn that all of us hunger for.
This legislation speaks to life. We want all of society to cherish the life that we propose here.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak to this bill, a bill that addresses an issue of the hearts, of the minds and souls of people. It is an issue in which we find very strongly held points of view on both sides.
There are those who would believe that this bill answers neither side of the question. It does not fully satisfy those who believe in a pro-choice point of view nor obviously, if one has just listened to our colleague, those who believe in a pro-life point of view. This is not the time in our society when one can afford to hold to one's personal conviction, which I would respect and hope that others would respect. I think it is a time to find a kind of compromise.
The question is: Does this bill answer the compromise that is required? I am still not very sure. I am still not 100 per cent comfortable with this bill.
This bill does respond to the jurisdiction question; it is a federal jurisdiction. It does define the act as a medical procedure. For that I am very pleased, for in the definition of a medical procedure it defines itself properly in the potential for access across this land. The question as to whether or not full access will be made available is one which I think will have to be looked at very carefully in legislative committee.
That women should have to consult their doctor, a medical practitioner, I believe to be sound. I believe that you do need to consult. The decision as to whether or not you wish to terminate a pregnancy is not an easy decision.
In fact I would suggest that the only time I would ever really enter into a very serious argument with colleagues who have a different point of view from mine is when they tell me that this act is one that a woman would undertake as an act of contraception. I find that to be very offensive. It is not an act of contraception. It is a very difficult emotional decision, one that is not easily taken. I would suggest that anyone who thinks otherwise has either never been pregnant or has not got very much
November 22, 1989

heart or is very hard minded in his or her own point of view.
I would suggest that being able to take an informed choice is very important. I would think being able to talk to a medical practitioner is helpful. I also believe it is very important that one have the best of health and the best of medical practice when a decision is taken, if the decision is taken to terminate her pregnancy. I believe the ultimate decision is that of the woman, but I do believe that she needs help and guidance. I trust the woman and the medical ethics of our medical profession.
The reservations I have about this bill and the reason I will vote to send it to legislative committee is that there are some issues that must be carefully examined. I do not know the answers, but I do know that there are concerns in this bill.
I believe that it needs careful scrutiny. I believe we must hear from the medical profession. I believe it must be checked to see if it will withstand a court challenge. I believe there are women who have to be heard.
While I support the full right of women to choose, I am well aware of the fact that others do not agree with this point of view. Because there are deeply held divisions in this society, there are no easy answers.
I would have preferred no law. When one lived through this past summer and saw the degradation and the stress that two cases before the courts underwent, the cases of Barbara Dodd and Chantal Daigle, one realized that there must be some form of legal format. Therefore, we cannot afford a country that is going to have 11 different laws and no sensible approach to this very difficult situation. The uncertainty is more than I think this society can withstand again. We certainly do not want that humiliation once again.
I am not happy that it has gone into the Criminal Code. I want to make very sure with legal counsel in legislative committee that there were sound reasons that it could not go under the Canada Health Act had it been amended. I understand and I accept the minister's perspective, but I would like to hear it once again.
I would hope if it absolutely must be recriminalized that we can find the mechanism through the Canada Health Act to ensure that access will be afforded all
Government Orders
women who take a decision, and not lightly, to terminate their pregnancies and to ensure that it can be met in every province and every town where this request is made.
I would suggest to you that there are a series of rights that come. With those rights come personal responsibility on behalf of the individual woman to make an enlightened decision early in her pregnancy. Equally there is the responsibility of the state to provide the means for a woman to take that decision, knowing that her society truly cares for her child, truly cares that these children will be brought up to be productive, well informed, well nourished, intelligent young people.
Our society has far from demonstrated that caring to date. We do not have the kind of support system or the cadre politique familial that we need.
We are in desperate need of a look at how we handle children in our society. There is violence against children, rape, incest, lack of decent food, lack of proper housing and child care. There is a lack of the kind of incentives that would help a woman make that enlightened choice.
I say to you that while rights and responsibilities go together, it is not only for the individual woman making that decision. It is not only for the individual doctor who is helping and counselling her. It is also for those of us who are legislators to determine what are the highest priorities in society and then direct those funds. It is not the death that is important. It is the life of these children.
I would suggest to you that we see this new law in the light of the concerns and constraints that many of us are expressing around this particular issue and that we try as best as possible to find the medium, the middle line. That road will not answer all our concerns. I am definitely one who would prefer a woman to be able to make that decision in an enlightened way and be solely responsible herself.
Those of you who feel that there should be no option, that life begins at conception and there are no other choices, will understand that we as legislators have to find something that will answer that need. We all live in a very pluralistic society today. We all come from very different backgrounds, upbringings and personal perspectives. For a woman who is about to make a choice, we must respect that choice but find the cadre in the

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
legislative perspective that will best meet her need and that of our society.
I have certain disappointments with the bill. There are certain aspects of the bill that I find acceptable. For goodness sakes, let us start to think about sex education in the schools. Sexuality is part of our humanity. We have to find a way to share the responsibilities of that sexuality, if it has to be through teaching in the schools because the parents cannot do it properly or teaching in whatever way or with whatever medium. It is important that they understand.
I would like to suggest that while I am pro-choice I find the best answer to meet the differences in our society will be the best response possible.
As one would say, as Canadians it is the best that is possible in a world of all possibilities. I will certainly vote to send this bill to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I must compliment you on your ability to listen attentively to the entreaties of all hon. members on the issue before this House, Bill C-43, what Canadians have come to regard as the abortion legislation.
I daresay that that ability must surely be taxed. I wonder whether in fact you are at all not unlike so many of our citizens, or even some of our colleagues, as argument, as philosophy, as emotion and, yes, even rhetoric buffet one's faculties from intervention to intervention. It calls up respect for the various positions explained by so many members who go through the tortuous ordeal in an effort to find a path so right, so true, so appropriate for a Canadian society that is, and for a Canadian society that is becoming.
Many colleagues have attempted the juridical approach to the question noting along the way that jurisprudence reflects social convention often following in the footsteps of accepted practice and rarely venturing into the realm of groundbreaking, in effect reflecting, and I quote a previous member, "things as they are and not as they should be".
It has been difficult to take umbrage with arguments of colleagues. They have been thoughtful and deliberate. They have been respectful of the need to be tolerant, I daresay, to the point of being obsequiously courteous to those whose arguments have been in diametric opposition to their own. Perhaps this is so because we all have a basic premise from which we launch ourselves in this debate. That premise, no matter what it is, is today faced with a dilemma as hon. colleagues espouse one position or another on the bill.
Examine if you will for a moment the consequences of voting no to this bill and carrying the vote. In so doing I might remind colleagues that of a most moving speech that I heard from an hon. member yesterday, a minister of the Crown, who reflected some, I beleive, widely held views, pointed to the "failings", the "deficiencies" and the "incompleteness" in this legislation, and still felt that a yes vote was required because the alternative to this bill was no law at all. No law means that those who advocate abortion on demand carry the day. Those who oppose this bill on the grounds that it is virtual abortion on demand are faced with a dilemma. I am such a one.
If we vote yes we accept in principle that abortion is undesirable. We acknowledge that anyone who wants one can have one, a medical practitioner accepting. Yet, there are no procedures imposed on the medical practitioner, no definitions of conduct, no guidelines of practice, no mechanism for adjudicating that practice.
In a word, the government has accepted that the question of abortion is merely a medical matter between a woman and her doctor. That is not what the government was encouraged to do when the Supreme Court struck down the old abortion legislation nearly two years ago. That ruling confirmed, perhaps positively I daresay-I hope positively-that women have universality of access to medical care.
It called on the government and Parliament to determine by way of legislation the rights of a foetus or unborn child, the extent to which those rights are equal to those already born, when those rights may take effect, whether and when the rights of the pregnant mother take precedence, and, if and when society or the state has an interest in the development of life in its foetal stage.
That ruling called on the government for leadership. It has shown none in this bill, nor has it heeded the call to be pro-active and to define life in a context different from that which is current, that is to say, one that sees no alternative to unrestricted abortion on demand. And
November 22, 1989

even, almost perversely I daresay, its caucus members, or some thereof, ask for support for this piece of legislation on the grounds-and in my view it is a little bit too clever by half-that, and I quote them, "the alternative will be the absence of any signal that there is any regard for the value of human life".
Government logic has abdicated the obligation to deal with life to the convenience of debating the issue of abortion and, I might add, in isolation of factors and social issues and policies that make abortion the attractive alternative to birth for many women.
Many hon. colleagues before me have detailed the lack of education on sex and on birth, the societal conditions that breed irresponsible sexual practices, carnal violence and disrespect for the dignity of women. They have spoken of the lack of affordable, accessible day care facilities and of the cost of raising a child by a single parent under the burden of increasing taxation or cutbacks in programs of a social support nature.
Other eloquent members have regretted the government's inaction in the face of the disintegration of the bulwark of social harmony and productivity: family cohesion and the values that emanate from it, that is, a sense of responsibility, a degree of compassion, a modicum of respect for others, mutual support in moments of crises and a long-term approach to actions and consequences.
Rather than show leadership on the question of life and on the quality thereof, the government has contented itself with casting the issue in the context of abortion, a context which invariably favours the rights of those who are present against those who are silent, a context which too often is seen as purely a woman's issue with the unfortunate consequence of pitting one gender against the other, a debate which attacks the contribution of someone like me as improper on gender, religious, cultural or legal grounds.
If we are what we have become as parliamentarians, then can the contribution to such a debate like that of this humble elected member, who is a married father of four, Christian Catholic, an educator and administrator in a constitutionally recognized separate school system which used to teach the family values of which I spoke a moment ago, an elected representative of the people
Government Orders
with the vested authority to promote the best interest of society, be so summarily dismissed? I say no.
We have all come here as parliamentarians to identify and define those values and conventions which distinguish Canadians and to legislate for conditions where these values and conventions are given nourishment to make our society a paragon of harmonious productive social interaction.
Yet with Bill C-43, on so fundamental a social issue the government abdicates to the medical profession its moral and legal responsibility to make decisions regarding life and/or abortion. It requires the provinces to pay for the services consequent to that decision of retaining the right to apply legal sanction under the Criminal Code in the event, unforeseeable today, that a doctor might be unable to satisfy the most generous of guidelines, that is, his or her own personal judgment.
No, our government has an obligation to present legislation that shows purpose and suggests direction. As parliamentarians we, too, then can discharge our obligation to debate the merits of that direction and a means to its realization. Regrettably this Bill C-43 gives us neither.
It asks us to debate legislation that inadequately deals with consequences. Bereft of vision it deprives us of the opportunity to address causes and goals. As such, it represents no compromise. It represents no solution. It is unworthy of support.

Madam Speaker, I have listened with great respect to the words of the previous speaker, the member for Eglinton-Lawrence. I thank him for them.
I also listened with great respect and admiration to the two speakers who preceded him. I would like to compliment the member for Mount Royal and my colleague, the member for Surrey-White Rock who spoke before her. From separate sides of the issue, they both gave sound, reasoned arguments. They are both to be commended on the strength and obvious sincerity of their presentations. It is a privilege for me to add my thoughts and words on this sensitive and emotional issue.
Each time one of us rises in this chamber to speak on any legislative change we accept a serious responsibility. While speaking we should always remain true to our own personal principles, but at the same time we should be

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
representing the views of those who elected us. We have to balance a requirement to provide leadership with the responsibility to represent the electorate.
Each of us puts a degree of thought, discussion and research into each and every topic that comes before us. I can think of no other issue that has come before this House in the time I have been here which has required the degree of thought and serious soul searching than the moral question of abortion.
To achieve political solutions to the complex and controversial problems that come before us it is often necessary to accept compromise. On this issue, however, views are held so strongly and opinions are so galvanized that many of the people we represent are, because of personal convictions, unwilling or unable to compromise their position or their belief. The same is true for many of the members who sit in this House.
Bill C-43 is by necessity a political answer to a moral question, and as a political answer represents a compromise and moral values are not subject to compromise.
My own personal and deeply held values are that life is sacred from the moment of conception right through until natural death. We do not have the right to murder. We do not want to take upon ourselves the right to take life from the elderly, the infirm or the mentally disabled. Rather we generously provide for their well-being through our envied system of social programs. We seek to enhance the quality of their lives and I question whether this bill does enough to protect the life of the unborn.
The bill does set a moral guideline, but I do not feel the definition of health is strict enough to dramatically reduce the number of abortions actually performed in this country.
Outside this House, and I appreciate that I have not heard it included in the debate, there are some who say that abortion is a women's issue and that men should refrain from commenting. I cannot agree with that. To deny men a voice is to perpetuate the myth that men have no responsibility for pregnancy. I do not accept that.
There is an unfortunate trend in this society of ours. On this and many other issues we ignore the requirement that we should all accept responsibility for our actions. As Canadians we have legislated and protected our rights, but if this society is going to continue to reflect the values upon which it was built, we have to understand and accept the fact that responsibility must precede and overshadow rights.
We are all too willing to demand our rights. Yet, at the same time, we are far too reluctant to assume the responsibilities that go with those rights. On this particular issue, it is essential to recognize that every sexually-active person should accept responsibility for his or her actions. Bill C-43 is an attempt to balance the rights of the mother to life and health with the rights of the unborn child.
In considering those rights, I cannot help but think of the uproar that would come if a newborn baby were discarded by its parents. I would suggest that there would be countless offers of support for such an infant. Canadians from coast to coast, regardless of their income level, religion or walk of life would open their hearts and homes to help and provide for that infant. I cannot comprehend how all those same people would not show that same degree of compassion and sympathy for the unborn.
At the same time, there is another side of the issue that we cannot overlook. When we talk of compassion, we must also be compassionate toward the mother, the woman with an unwanted pregnancy. We who advocate life for the unborn have a responsibility to provide not only compassion but also economic, social and cultural support for that mother. We must provide her with choices, choices other than abortion. We have to enhance an adoption alternative. We should be willing to provide her with economic and moral support so that we encourage and enable her to continue with an unplanned and unwanted pregnancy.
It has been said by almost everybody in this debate that abortion should not be accepted as a form of birth control. In excess of 65,000 therapeutic abortions were performed in Canada last year. This is far too many. Abortion has become a far too commonly accepted procedure.
We also have to accept the sad fact that no law is going to stop abortion completely. A law cannot change the
November 22, 1989

human heart. It is not going to achieve what society is unwilling to accept. Attitudes and values have to change. Those attitudes and values are formed not in legislation but in our families, our churches and our communities.
Bill C-43 does make a very important statement. It recognizes that life is sacred from the moment of conception and that it does not gain value with age. It sets a moral tone which says that Canada does not condone abortions and because it recognizes that life is sacred from the moment of conception, it should be protected, the only exception being when the health of the mother is threatened.
In a perfect world there would be no need for a law, but our world is far from perfect and Canadians are demanding a law. They will not tolerate another series of court challenges similar to those we have seen in the past year. On the 293 of us in this Chamber falls the responsibility to set a standard for Canadians. Yet within this Chamber and within Canada there is no unanimity. There is no clear consensus as to the perfect law, so we have to compromise. We have to decide whether Canadians will accept a compromise and whether those who hold to either side of the question in this House will accept a compromise.
My decision has come down to two questions. First, is no law better than one that is less than perfect? Second, what is the purpose of the law? With regard to the first question, we have seen what no law can do. I do not want to see a repeat of last summer's series of court challenges, nor do I feel will Canadians accept a decision from us that allows a repeat of those challenges.
More important is the second question. What is the purpose of the law? I have said, and I would hope everyone would accept, that we cannot legislate morality. We cannot change individual values through legislation. What we can do with the law is to set a standard. Beyond that, we must encourage our communities, our churches, our families and individual Canadians to take responsibility for influencing moral values. Although this legislation will not change what is within a person's heart, it can enforce the need for reflection and emphasize the seriousness of action.
It has been stated by some that the bill will restrict a woman's access to abortion. Those on the same side of the issue as myself fear that in reality the definition of
Government Orders
health is too broad and there would be too few restrictions.
We need to set a standard and this is not the law that I would prefer to see. I support a more restrictive definition of health. I have decided after much soul-searching that I will vote for this bill on second reading. Further to that, I will also be urging those who truly love life to encourage others who share that love to help provide support with compassion for those with unwanted pregnancies, to help provide choices for them other than abortion.

Madam Speaker, I begin by regretting that those of us who participate in the debate at this time in the process have only 10 minutes. I truly feel that it would take me about three hours and 10 minutes to explain everything that there is in my own mind about this issue. Regardless of what I have to say tonight, it is bound to be somewhat truncated, incomplete and therefore inarticulate.
It is also the case that I wish all of the debates that we have in this House were of the quality which we are having on this particular issue. I do not want to use up too much time on this, but this is the kind of debate that those of us who participated in the McGrath committee process had in mind for a wider range of issues in the House. Although, frankly, I do not know if I could stand it if we had a lot of debate like this, because this issue is so very, veiy difficult. It is certainly an issue which has caused me personally no end of personal and intellectual hell since my first election campaign in 1979.
There was a time when I would have wanted to support this bill. It contains elements of what, at one time, I thought would be close to a solution. I used to say to some of my friends when we were talking about this, that what was needed was a form of decent hypocrisy when it came to this issue; that what we needed was something which was pro-life in substance and prochoice in practice; that most Canadians were concerned not so much about the number of abortions that were taking place but about the preservation of certain values and about the preservation of the notion of their being value in unborn life. To a certain extent, this bill does that. In fact, it was described by the hon. member for Kitchener the other day, as being pro-life in substance and pro-choice in practice. It is in that respect that I

November 22, 1989
Government Orders
wonder why so many pro-life members have decided to vote for it but I think I understand what they are doing.
I have arrived after much travail at a view that regards the use of the criminal law as unacceptable with respect to the regulation of abortion. I said this last summer, it is not something that I am saying for the first time, whether we like it or not, the criminal law is an instrument of power and an instrument of coercion. After much struggle I have come to see that much of what this debate is about is power. It is about the power relationships, if you like, between women and men; between women and society. The use of the criminal power in this case, regardless of whether it is ever used, represents a continuing offence against what so many women regard as their rightful self-consciousness as an individual person when it comes to this kind of intensely private decision.
I think the use of the criminal law is inappropriate in this case. I would have hoped that some other way could have been found. I continue to believe that many of the abortions which will be chosen, either in the context of this law if it is passed or in the context of there being no law, will be the wrong choices. I do not think that choices just by virtue of the fact that they are free choices are therefore the right decisions. But I have come to the conclusion that these right or wrong decisions have to be taken by the women involved and not by doctors and not by the state.
I could sum up my position by saying that I think the pro-choice people are right, in many cases for the wrong reasons. I have found much of the rhetoric and many of the assumptions underlying the arguments of the prochoice position to be faulty and to contain assumptions which I reject, but as a policy, not as an inalienable exalted right, I believe that this is the way that we have to go at this point in history.
Having said that the pro-choice people were right in many cases for the wrong reasons, I also think the pro-life people are wrong for all the right reasons. Many of the things they say are values which all of us here want to uphold. Where we disagree is about whether or not those values can in fact be upheld in the way in which they want them to be upheld, through the power of the criminal law.
The law is not just a force, it is also a teacher. So I accept the argument that when we are talking about law
we are talking about values. But we can give a signal about the value we put on unborn life, on children and on families in so many other ways. We can do it by not trying to de-index family allowances. We can do it by a massive attack on child poverty. We can do it in a myriad of different social and economic ways. We can send signals to perspective parents that life, in this case unborn and then young life, is something which we value. Presently, we do not send out those signals very well at all.
I might have been persuaded because I have long advocated a compromise. But, as you can see, I have changed my mind. I might have been more tempted if the compromise had provided an anxiety free period. That is to say, some period in which there might have been a complete pro-choice policy moving to a more restrictive approach in the latter part of the pregnancy. However, I am convinced, because I have had a good look at the CMA guidelines and other medical regulations, that abortions in the third trimester after viability are very rare indeed. And they should be. If it ever came to my attention that this was not the case then I would be the first one to argue that there ought to be some sanction against that practice. Yet, there just does not seem to be any evidence that there is a need for that kind of interference at this point.
One member said, and I agree, that we should never be in the situation where, in one wing of the hospital we are striving to save a premature baby and in the other wing of the hospital we are, by virtue of whatever policy we adopt, condoning the termination of the life of foetuses which are at the same stage as those who have been born prematurely.
This is where I am after 10 years of very, very difficult thinking about this. I retain my willingness to be critical of the arguments put forward by both sides in this debate. I think that in many cases, unfortunately, both the pro life and the pro choice positions have been presented in a way which is so symptomatic of our times, as a kind of instant quick-fix solution to problems which run much deeper.
The pro life forces, particularly those who operate from a religious perspective, want to have a world without sin. It cannot be done. Many of the pro choice forces want to have a world without guilt. That cannot be done either. We can have a world in which the privacy, the dignity and the intimacy which women deserve in these kinds of decisions is respected.
November 22, 1989

In the absence of the government coming forward with a bill that really tries to address some of these very difficult issues, particularly issues which I think will have to be addressed down the road with respect to early-stage abortions, when technology permits us to make more choices, not just about whether or not to have a child but what kind of child to have, questions which are not being addressed in this debate and will have to be addressed by people on both sides, sooner or later-
In the meantime, the government having failed to do that, but having succeeded in doing what I think the hon. member from Victoria said so well in coming forward with a bill to protect politicians, something under which a majority of us could huddle for protection from the various groups that have such strong opinions on this, my only alternative is to vote against the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with mixed emotions. I feel relieved that we are finally seeing legislation introduced on abortion, but I must say that it saddens me deeply that at this juncture in what we believe to be our highly evolved society, we need to be debating whether we should have legislation that provides guidelines for abortion. In my view, and in the view of the majority of my constituents, there is no question guidelines are needed.
In my home province of British Columbia there are 26 abortions for every 100 live births. Yes, guidelines are needed. All members of this House, and in fact most members of the Canadian public are aware of the controversy that surrounds this issue. In fact there have been a great number of court cases involving abortion.
The most recent case that has been decided comes from the Supreme Court of Canada. As members will know, it is the Chantal Daigle case. Although decided on August 8, the court has only recently provided us with the reasons for its decision. Once again, the main message of the court comes through loud and clear. That message states that the responsibility lies on our shoulders. We, the legislators, must take action. The court does not exist to make law. There is no government by
Government Orders
judiciary in Canada. The Supreme Court has not ventured into the realm of making law, but to its credit leaves that to the members who are gathered here. Now we are doing just that.
I am aware that there appears to be a great movement to block any action on this important issue. Once again, common sense is not so common. Nonetheless, that movement is, to my understanding, a vocal minority. The silent majority, whom I believe share my concern, are tired of waiting. They elected us to the House of Commons to take action. That is what we are doing. Some say that Bill C-43 returns us to what we had before the 1988 Supreme Court decision on Morgentaler. Some say that we will have abortion on demand. I disagree. There are three points that must be made clear.
First, by introducing a law that provides guidelines for abortion, the government is indicating that the state has an interest in the foetus.
Second, by avoiding a gestational approach, the government is recognizing that life begins at conception. If this were not the case, then the state would have no reason to regulate abortion.
Third, and most important, I believe that this legislation will stand up to a challenge in the Supreme Court of Canada. The ability to stand up to a court challenge is essential. We presently have no legal guidelines for abortion because the Supreme Court found the previous law to be unconstitutional.
The present situation of no regulation has been recognized as unacceptable. It is tantamount to anarchy. To enact a law that would subsequently fall, if challenged, would be irresponsible as it would simply result in the present anarchic situation. I find the present situation of no legislation to be unacceptable. We need a law to protect the unborn. This bill is that law. It is a step in the right direction. This is true for several reasons. It recognizes that life begins at conception. There has been no attempt at negotiating this point. By avoiding the gestational approach, the government is saying that a foetus, the unborn, is protected by the state and by the law from conception onward.
Because life begins at conception and the state has an interest in that life, the method which exists to unnatu-

Government Orders
rally terminate that life, namely, abortion, is being controlled. This control has not been introduced in a vacuum. On the contrary, the government has learned that the Supreme Court will strike down any unconstitutional laws. Therefore, the government has provided for the rights of the woman by allowing abortion in the cases of physical, mental and psychological threats to the woman's health. This is consistent with the Charter. It does not coerce a woman to bear children under penalty of law. At the same time, it does not allow the woman to have access to abortion on demand. The balance that is apparent in Bill C-43 is consistent with our Constitution. It is not contrary, and if challenged, I believe it will not fall.
I am here in this House today at the behest of the electors of Fraser Valley East. It is only fitting to make reference to the prevailing feeling that exists in my constituency. The people of Fraser Valley East are overwhelmingly on the side of the unborn.
When I stood for election in 1984 and re-election in 1988 I did so on a highly visible platform that included among other things a pro-life component. My beliefs were not secret. The electors of Fraser Valley East knew my record on the issue of abortion. They were well aware of the position I would take and they knew the reasons why. I was not then, nor am I now, a one-issue politician. I made a commitment to influence policy. They accepted that commitment. They knew that I would not change the world. The commitment was made and it has been kept. My constituents know me and they know my position. They voted accordingly and here I am. What is it that they think on this very important issue? Like myself and many other members in this House, they think that life begins at conception. They believe that life is sacred and although concessions are part and parcel of politics there can be no compromise on these principles.
Church and state are separate. The state must be all things to all people. This is what we must hold true if we are to have the understanding and tolerant society we say we desire. This involves being true to certain underlying principles that make the existence of the state possible. Among those principles of tolerance and understanding are the principles of the preservation and sanctity of life.
This is true regardless of religion or the absence thereof. That is why it was so important that this bill did not take the gestational approach. The gestational approach is simply indefensible. It draws an arbitrary dividing line between life, which is worthy of protection and life, which is not. It ignores a primary function of law, the protection of human life. There can be no compromise on the principle of when life begins. The foetus is protected from conception and that is evident in this bill.
In politics and in a plural society we realize that concessions must be made. Reality tells us that compromise is necessary.
The oft-quoted example of the British parliamentarian, William Wilberforce, and his 17-year struggle to abolish slavery stands as testimony to the need and indeed the efficacy of compromise. I might point out that it is compromise on the means not the end. The principle must remain intact.
A gestational approach is unacceptable because it would betray the principles of recognizing that life begins at conception and that life is sacred. This principle has not been compromised and that is why this legislation is a positive step in the right direction. That is why I can support this bill and believe that my constituents, although they might not be completely satisfied with this bill, would accept it. Like William Wilberforce I am willing to fight the good fight for my principles.
Although I can support this bill I do have reservations. I believe the bill would be more effective with more demanding definitions of the kinds of health risks that merit access to abortion. But it is at committee, or report stage, when we must try to strengthen the provisions of this bill and propose suitable amendments.
We need a law to protect the unborn. Having no law is unacceptable because I believe that life does begin at conception. Bill C-43 recognizes this fact. This recognition is the only reason that I can support this legislation. It is for this and the aforementioned reasons that I support this bill and I encourage other members to do likewise. The legislative committee must study this piece of legistative and report back to this House.
November 22, 1989

THE BUDGET-REQUEST FOR BUDGET WITHDRAWAL-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on April 28, I raised questions in the House with the Minister of Finance about the budget leaks. That was a long time ago. Since then charges were laid and the sub judice convention has been applied by the Speaker for the time being. I want to respect that. However, I want to use the opportunity here to make a very important point about the way in which this government sees its responsibility.
What I want to point out through the answers we have received to questions on a number of subjects over the last few months is that the government no longer assumes any responsibility for its moral conduct, for the proper administration of the public affairs, or for the proper discharge of the duties of ministers. The government is not prepared to give any indication of how its own responsibilities are discharged, except in one way, and that is to say if members on this side of the House have any evidence of wrong-doing we should go to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In other words, the conscience of this government has disintegrated and declined to the lowest level of behavior in the country. If it is criminal behaviour, it has nothing to say about it. Its colleagues are to be presumed innocent until proven guilty. In the meanwhile, if we have any evidence that any of them is breaking the law, we should take that to the police.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE BUDGET-REQUEST FOR BUDGET WITHDRAWAL-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S RESIGNATION
speechtext: It sounds reasonable to me.

subtopic: THE BUDGET-REQUEST FOR BUDGET WITHDRAWAL-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Well, it may sound reasonable to the members opposite, but I understood when this present government was elected that it would operate at a level, not only which would be beyond reproach, but which would also appear to be beyond reproach. Ministers would not only behave according to the highest moral standards, which are much higher, by the way, than the
Adjournment Debate
standards of the criminal law, and they would appear to operate by them.
I took that to mean that when a minister or a member of the House came under a legitimate cloud of suspicion that the minister or the member would do the honourable thing while matters were being investigated, and not necessarily only those on a criminal basis. It could well simply be a breach of an undertaking, or conduct legal but unbecoming a member of the government. In that connection, I think that the public administration of Canada has deteriorated enormously under this government.
I asked about the budget leak and whether there was a state of sloppiness existing around security in the preparation of the budget. I was not necessarily talking about criminal behaviour. I did not know whether a crime had been committed in the way in which the budget was prepared and the level of security that was applied to it. I was simply asking whether the standard of security in the operations of the Queen's Printer, under the responsibility of standards which cover a number of ministries, were adequate. That is a simple question. It is not asking for a criminal investigation. The answer that I got on April 28 was: "Investigations are being conducted, Mr. Speaker, and it is entirely inappropriate to comment on them in this House". That was the answer on April 28.
Today I read a Canadian Press release, reported in nearly every newspaper in Canada, including The Globe and Mail which states:
Budget leak investigation ended.
The RCMP has concluded all its investigations into the leak of Finance Minister Michael Wilson's budget and does not plan to lay any more charges.
Federal Solicitor-General Pierre Blais told reporters-
-(that he did not know whether the investigations were still under way).
But Sergeant Pierre Belanger, an RCMP spokesman, said-" We have no evidence of any wrongdoing. No charges will be laid".
The excuse for not answering my question, and I quote again from Hansard: "Investigations are being conducted, Mr. Speaker, and it is entirely inappropriate to comment on them in this House."
Well, I never accepted that answer. Even if I had accepted it, the validity of that answer expires today, November 22, 1989, because according to the RCMP, investigations are now concluded. So I want to ask the representative of the minister the question that I asked which could not be answered as it was answered back in

November 22, 1989
Adjournment Debate
April when the excuse was given that criminal investigations were under way, as if that had everything to do with the question I was asking.
Will the minister confirm that a state of sloppiness existed around the security in the preparation of his budget? On the basis of that sloppy security, will he tell us whether he will recognize his responsibility for it?
