Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity tonight to return to the issue of the northern air stage parcel subsidy which I raised in the House on October 27.
For the past several years going back at least to the 1970s, Canada Post has been delivering food stuff and other goods to remote communities in certain provinces and the Northwest Territories. It has been delivering these goods at a rate which is much lower than air freight
rates. This service is known as the northern air stage parcel subsidy.
This service means that northern residents can purchase basic groceries and other essential goods at prices that, while still much higher than what the goods would cost in a southern Canadian city, are still much cheaper than goods delivered under commercial air cargo rates.
Previous governments subsidized Canada Post for providing this service with an annual funding allotment. They did so in order to fulfil an important public policy goal and social objective. Previous governments wanted residents in the northern and most remote parts of Canada to have access to fresh produce, fruits and vegetables and other basic groceries and goods throughout the year at reasonable and affordable prices.
The current Conservative government has abandoned this social policy objective. In 1986, without consultation with northerners, it decided to phase out the subsidy. Since 1986, the subsidy has declined by $1 million a year. The government's intention is to eliminate the subsidy totally within 15 years.
Because the subsidy has been reduced, Canada Post has decided that it must raise the northern air stage parcel rates by an average of 32 per cent. Eighty-five communities in the Northwest Territories and the northern parts of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan will be hurt by this increase. Twenty-three of those affected communities are in my constituency in the eastern Arctic.
A letter from Arctic Co-Operatives Limited to the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs, and the minister responsible for Canada Post, says the rate changes will have a devastating effect on the people of the north.
According to the Arctic Co-operatives, this increase means that a case of bread, now $21.49, will increase to $41.30. A case of baby's powder formula, now $13.41, will increase to $41.30. A case of Pampers, now $25.65, will increase to $56.10.
In the community of Broughton Island a loaf of bread now costs $3.45. After the increase, that same loaf of bread is going to cost $4.49. A head of lettuce now costs
November 22, 1989

$4.27. After the increase that lettuce is going to cost $5.55.
Would the members of the government and the officials of Canada Post like to pay almost $6 for a bunch of celery? What about $5 for two pounds of carrots? Even with their high salaries they would find it difficult. For the people in these remote northern communities where unemployment rates are 50 per cent and higher and most people are on fixed incomes, these prices are absolutely beyond reach. People will not be able to feed their families properly. People, including children, are going to go without. There will be health consequences and severe emotional and financial hardship and stress placed on families. These will be the results of this callous and heartless government position.
On November 2 I attended a meeting with officials from Canada Post, Indian and Northern Affairs, Health and Welfare and the hon. member from Abitibi. Also at that meeting were representatives from northern Indian and Inuit communities and groups. The meeting ended with a request from aboriginal representatives for a moratorium of one year on the proposed rate increase.
Late that evening, Canada Post issued a press release postponing the implementation of the increase from November 13 to January 31, 1990. Between November 2 and January 31 consultation is to take place with affected parties to minimize the impact of the increase.
The following day, November 3,1 questioned government ministers about the postponement and was told that a working group would be set up to deal with the issues. Since that day, November 3,1 have been trying to get more information on this working group. As of this afternoon, no one could tell me who is chairing the group. For almost three weeks Canada Post and Indian and Northern Affairs have been fighting over who will take the lead role. Canada Post does not want the lead role. It says Indian and Northern Affairs should have it. Indian and Northern Affairs does not want this responsibility. It says the program is Canada Post's.
Since the departments cannot agree on who will lead it, the study group is not yet officially established. Since it is not officially established, it has no terms of reference. The terms of reference will be worked out when the group meets. When will it meet? No one knows
Adjournment Debate
because it has not been officially established. Will there be representatives from the affected northern communities? No one can say because it will have to be discussed when the group meets and no one knows when that will be.
Due to this infighting we have already lost about three weeks of the three months that were supposed to be used for consultation. Who suffers from this delay? Not Canada Post, not Indian and Northern Affairs. But the people of the north.
Three months is too short a time to begin with. Christmas is coming and not much work will get done during the Christmas season. The postponement it seems is just an executioner's delay. Canada Post appears determined to proceed with this increase. It says it cannot continue to provide the service at current rates because of the cut-back to the subsidy.
An acceptable solution will not be found by January 31 without clear and precise political direction from the ministers who are involved. The proposed increase must be stopped, not merely postponed. The government must reverse a decision it took in 1986 to eliminate the subsidy. This increase is not justified. We have had no roads built in the eastern Arctic which would enable us to bring in our groceries more cheaply than by air; our frozen waters will not permit year round shipping. We will not accept a situation where we can have fresh fruit and vegetables during the summer months only when the ships can come in.
The government has no major economic development plans for the eastern Arctic which would increase employment and incomes. With all the tax increases over the past few years and the new proposed goods and services tax scheduled for 1991, northern incomes and standards of living are being further set back, and to put an increase of 32 per cent on basic groceries and foodstuff is absolutely intolerable.
I urge the Ministers of Indian and Northern Affairs, Canada Post and Health and Welfare to go back to their cabinet colleagues. Tell them that you did not realize how devastating this increase would be upon the northern people. Tell them the subsidy must not be eliminated, that it must be maintained at a level that will not result in Canada Post increasing its rates.

November 22, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Tell them that children, single mothers, elderly pensioners, and unemployed youth will suffer the most. Ask them if they are truly willing to reduce the deficit on the backs of these people whose only offence is that they live in the north. Ask them to please put people ahead of profits.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq has outlined the problem very clearly and he has also discussed tonight what appears to be a problem in getting on with the solution to the problem.
Several points have to be made. First, the role of Canada Post must be to provide delivery services across this country. Beyond that, when we get heavily into social policy, that rightly falls to other areas. I noted in the conclusion of the member's remarks, when he was talking about the impact of this decision with respect to the northern air stage rate increases, that this was going to be on the backs of the elderly, single mothers and so on.
I understand the concerns. The member speaks very eloquently about them, but I do not believe those are matters that fall within the ambit of Canada Post and they are much more correctly dealt with under other government programs. That is the reason that a joint or interdepartmental committee has been proposed. Two months remain before the rate increases go into effect. I would hope that is time enough for all the interested parties to get together. The hon. member says that time has already gone by before this committee has found which table it is sitting at and who is going to be bringing down the gavel as chairman. I submit to him and to those he represents that already since this announcement was made by the government on November 2 there is a delay in the increase until the end of January. This is to provide time for consultation with northerners so that those in the north and others have an opportunity to get their suggestions and proposals together. I am sure that his intervention in the House tonight is going to accelerate the process of getting that committee struck and I do think it will also be an opportunity for some of the uncertainty about this to be clarified.
I know the hon. member speaks on all his examples in graphic terms specifically about the increase of items at the retail level. In fact, the proposed rate increase will be
applied of the basis of the per kilogram weight and whether that translates into the price increases that have been described in the House tonight is something that is going to have to be reviewed by this committee.
The issue is an important one. The reality of northern distribution of goods and services, and this is not through a service that is like the distribution of parcels normally through Canada Post but the special operation of northern air stage, is a unique service for a unique part of Canada. That is why the government has held back on the effort to try to have the post office in all parts of Canada from coast to coast pay its way and be responsible in delivery of services to people but with all Canadians, wherever they live, paying their fair share. It is never easy, but I hope with the co-operation of the hon. member and certainly the impetus that he has given tonight to get this interdepartmental committee moving that we can get a good result in a balanced way.
TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS/EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

Madam Speaker, I rise following a question which I put on October 25 to the Minister of State for Transport. It deals with the transportation on B.C. ferries of hazardous materials and, in particular, PCBs. This issue was first raised in August by the President of the B.C. Ferry and Marine Workers Union, Lee Cochrane. It had come to the attention of the union that PCBs and other dangerous goods were being carried on B.C. passenger ferries, and that this was happening without any inspection to see whether the regulations were being complied with.
It emerged that, in fact, the Department of Transport had imposed restrictions and conditions on the transportation of dangerous cargoes on passenger ferries 18 months ago. But it also was quickly conceded by the regional people that, in fact, they did not have the staff to see whether the conditions were even being complied with. There was apparently no requirement being placed on terminal agents and others to ensure that when a truck carrying a dangerous cargo or PCBs came on a B.C. ferry that the regulations were being complied with. No notice was being given and nothing was happening to see that these very detailed lists of conditions were being met.
November 22, 1989

When I asked the minister about this back toward the end of October, the minister's reply was that we have great conditions, we have checked them all out and the conditions and restrictions are adequate, which of course, missed the point. The point was not the adequacy of the conditions. The point was the adequacy of the enforcement of the conditions.
The matter then got raised in the Auditor General's report, because as it happens the Auditor General was digging into this very situation. In his report this year he came through with a devastating attack on Transport Canada for precisely this point and others, namely, that there was not sufficient staff to inspect dangerous cargoes on ferries.
What we are looking at here is trying to prevent a disaster before it happens. This is not a partisan issue. This is one which I am sure the department is as concerned about as we are on this side of the House. What we have here is a failure on the part of Treasury Board and others in government to ensure that personnel resources are available to inspect and ensure that these regulations are being maintained.
One would have thought after all that the department would have got the message. Just the other day I received a letter from the Minister of Transport, and the minister replies finally to my September 15 letter. I received this in my office on November 1, 1989. In this reply all we got was the same old stuff: "I must emphasize that the conditions imposed were more stringent than those required by the IMDG Code or the Dangerous Goods Shipping Regulations. The Canadian Coast Guard is enforcing all such regulatory requirements." That is just not true. It is not enforcing the requirements.
What I would ask the parliamentary secretary to do is to at least acknowledge an understanding of the problem and assure the people of Vancouver Island and those who travel on B.C. Ferries-and this issue probably applies to other ferries across Canada, but we know it applies on the coast-that the government understands the problem, that the problem is grasped by the department, that there is some plan in motion to try to get the necessary inspection resources in place, that the government is going to inform B.C. Ferries staff, or require that they be informed before these shipments take place, and that there is going to be some system of inspection. The Auditor General said that the only inspections that take place are kind of annual inspections. The ferries and
Adjournment Debate
others are warned they are coming and that is all that happens. But there are no unpredictable spot visits.
You have had notice of this. What we ask is that the department at least acknowledge this and say that something is going to be done. In the meantime, lift the permission. No hardship is going to occur if for a two or three-month period permission to transport on passenger ferries is lifted because there are other ways of getting dangerous goods back and forth from Vancouver Island. They can be carried on non-passenger vessels.
So please, we ask, that you at least acknowledge the problem and give the people of Vancouver Island some assurance that this matter is going to be dealt with.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to address this House on the important issue raised by the hon. member for Victoria on the adequacy of the Coast Guard program to ensure that dangerous goods are safely carried on passenger ferries.
First, let me state that the health and safety of the travelling public remains a top priority of this government. With this in mind, Coast Guard inspection procedures are constantly being reviewed to ensure that marine transportation of dangerous goods in Canadian waters are effectively and efficiently controlled and monitored.
In his report, the Auditor General made specific references to the dangerous goods inspections, procedures currently being employed by the Coast Guard on vessels of either Canadian or foreign registry. The transportation of dangerous goods by any mode is subject to very strict regulations. Under the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act anyone transporting dangerous goods in defiance of the act is breaking the law.
The transportation of packaged dangerous goods by ferry is regulated by both the dangerous goods shipping regulations made under the Canada Shipping Act and the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and regulations.
The Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and the regulations address the classifications, marking and documentation requirements, while the dangerous goods shipping regulations address the stowage and segregation of dangerous goods aboard the ferry.
The Auditor General has noted in his report that we do investigate and conduct inspections on ferries when some specific concern exists and random inspections are also conducted.
The Coast Guard also conducts training courses for senior officers and shore management officials to ensure a full and complete knowledge of regulatory

November 22, 1989
Adjournment Debate
requirements, including particularly reference to the types of dangerous goods prohibited on passenger ferries and those other dangerous goods that may be subject to stowage restrictions. In addition, Coast Guard inspectors are available to provide advice and guidance to ferry safety supervisors.
The department will continue to work closely with other jurisdictions to continue to improve upon the safe transportation of dangerous goods. It should be pointed out that the Auditor General stated that the Coast
Guard's mandatory inspection of safety features, regulations and examinations of mariners is well organized and well carried out.
